41: =dist(euclideanLift(x,t),euclideanLift(y,u))².
42: Distances are nonnegative, so equality of squares gives equality of distances. This proves an isometry into Euclidean ℝ^(n+1); truncation of the first n coordinates and extraction of the last coordinate give its inverse. For n=0 the sum is empty and the same construction is the usual identification of ℝ^0×ℝ with ℝ. It sends euclideanLift '' (E×I) exactly to the original Euclidean product set. value.statement: For every metric space X, subset A⊆X and real a>0, the positive-scale contents C^a_δ(A) are exactly the unnormalized real-diameter countable-cover contents of the original problem. Finite or countable index families can be reindexed into ℕ with empty padding and unchanged cost. For 0<δ₁≤δ₂, C^a_δ₂(A)≤C^a_δ₁(A). Each admissible δ-cover has cost at least C^a_δ(A), and every lower bound for all admissible costs bounds C^a_δ(A) below (including when no cover exists). H^a(A)=sup_{δ>0} C^a_δ(A), so C^a_δ(A)≤H^a(A). For δ>0, C^a_δ(A)=0 iff for every real ε>0 there is an admissible countable δ-cover with a-cost <ε. Consequently H^a(A)=0 iff such covers exist at every positive δ and every positive ε. All costs and infima are in ℝ≥0∞; empty members contribute zero.

Fix A⊆X.
Fix real a; temporarily assume L1: a>0.
Fix an arbitrary real scale δ; positive-scale uses are under the stated local antecedents.
Fix an arbitrary real tolerance ε; positivity is the local antecedent in S002.
In the extended-scale comparison let r range over positive extended scales; its finite and infinite cases are treated explicitly.

For the scale-monotonicity proof fix any real δ₂.

argument.text: Fix X,A,a and assume L1: a>0. Work with X's Borel structure, so M001 applies and gives H^a(A)=sup_{r>0} content(a,r,A) over extended nonnegative r. For arbitrary δ, temporarily assume L2: δ>0. At the finite scale ofReal δ, every admissible covering member has finite extended diameter, hence is bounded and has ediam equal to its real diameter cast to ℝ≥0∞. The nonemptiness-proof supremum in D004 is the displayed diameter power on a nonempty member and is zero on an empty member. For a>0 this agrees with assigning the empty member diameter zero and 0^a=0. Thus the nested infima are exactly the original admissible-cover infimum, with no prefactor. A finite family can be padded by empty sets. For an arbitrary countable index type choose an injection into ℕ; at each image index put the unique original member and elsewhere put ∅. This preserves the union and all nonnegative sums. Conversely an ℕ-family is countable. Discharge L2 after this finite-scale interpretation, retaining its δ>0 antecedent for every δ. For arbitrary δ₁,δ₂, temporarily assume L3: 0<δ₁≤δ₂. Every δ₁-cover is a δ₂-cover, so C^a_δ₂(A)≤C^a_δ₁(A). Discharge L3 and quantify the two scales. Every cost bounds its infimum above; a lower bound on every admissible cost bounds the infimum below. If the admissible family is empty its infimum is ∞, and the latter assertion remains true. For any positive extended scale r, if it is finite it is the cast of a positive real scale. The content at r=∞ is at most that at any fixed finite positive scale, since every finite-scale cover is also an ∞-cover. Hence the ∞ scale adds nothing to the supremum. We have proved H^a(A)=sup_{δ>0}C^a_δ(A), and each such content is ≤H^a(A).

produces.statement: Under a>0, the contents have the real-diameter countable-cover interpretation with empty padding/reindexing; they are nonincreasing in positive scale, satisfy the two infimum bounds, and H^a(A)=sup_{δ_bound>0}C^a_{δ_bound}(A).

argument.text: For the arbitrary δ,ε, temporarily assume L4: δ>0 and ε>0. Suppose L5: C^a_δ(A)=0. if every admissible cost were ≥ε, the lower-bound property in F001 would imply C^a_δ(A)≥ε>0, a contradiction. Thus an admissible cover of cost <ε exists. Discharge L5 to obtain the forward implication. In terms of the nested infima in D004, any failed cover or diameter condition has value ∞ and cannot give a value <ε, so the approximation provides an actual admissible family. Conversely assume L6: for every positive tolerance there exists an admissible cover of smaller cost. This forces the nonnegative content to be zero: a positive value, finite or infinite, has some positive finite real below it, contradicting the upper bound by those costs. Discharge L6, then L4, and quantify the arbitrary positive scale and tolerance. This proves the zero-content approximation equivalence for every positive scale. These arguments also cover an empty admissible family, whose content is ∞.

produces.statement: For every δ_bound>0, C^a_{δ_bound}(A)=0 iff at every positive finite real tolerance there exists an admissible countable δ_bound-cover of A of smaller a-cost.

argument.text: By F001, H^a(A)=0 implies each positive-scale content is zero; F002 then gives the required arbitrarily small covers at every scale. Conversely, those covers make every positive-scale content zero by F002, and their supremum is zero by F001. This proves the full equivalence and all asserted content properties. Discharge L1 to retain a>0 as an antecedent and universally quantify X,A,a and the scale/tolerance variables. No boundedness or measurability assumption on A is used.

applications.bindings: Take W=X with its Borel structure, exponent a and set A; expand the extended-scale content exactly as D004.

argument.text: Fix X,A,q and assume L1: q>0 and H^q(A)=0. Fix arbitrary real δ,ε and assume L2: δ>0 and ε>0. Put r=min(1,δ), so 0<r≤1 and r≤δ. By N001 with exponent q, scale r and tolerance ε/4 there exists a countable r-cover U of A whose total q-cost is <ε/4; reindex it as a sequence with empty padding if necessary. In particular its members have finite diameter.

argument.text: Choose U from F001 and put d_i=diam(U_i), with d_i=0 on empty members. For each natural i define a_seq(i)=min(r,(ε·2^(-i-3))^(1/q)). Both entries of this minimum are positive, so 0<a_seq(i)≤r and a_seq(i)^q≤ε·2^(-i-3). The nonnegative geometric series has sum Σ_{i≥0}2^(-i-3)=1/4 (its partial sums are (1/4)(1-2^(-m)) for the first m terms). Hence Σ a_seq(i)^q≤ε/4. Put r_i=max(d_i,a_seq(i)). Then 0<r_i≤r≤1 and r_i^q=max(d_i^q,a_seq(i)^q)≤d_i^q+a_seq(i)^q. Summing nonnegative terms, using F001 and the geometric bound, gives Σ r_i^q<ε/2. Numerical padding changes no covering set and works even if X is a singleton.

produces.statement: U covers A, d_i=diam(U_i)≤r_i, and 0<r_i≤r≤min(1,δ) for all natural i; Σ_i r_i^q<ε/2.

argument.text: For each natural i put N_i=ceil(1/r_i), a positive integer. Then 1/N_i≤r_i and N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i, since 0<r_i≤1. The closed intervals [h/N_i,(h+1)/N_i], 0≤h<N_i, cover I. Define W_seq(i,h)=U_i×[h/N_i,(h+1)/N_i]. In the maximum product metric any two points of this product have distance at most r_i, since the first-coordinate diameter is d_i≤r_i and the second-coordinate interval length is 1/N_i≤r_i. The product family covers A×I, and its index set {(i,h):i∈ℕ,0≤h<N_i} is countable. Empty products have zero cost. By N001 this countable family may be reindexed into ℕ without changing the union or sum. It is a δ-cover, and its total (q+1)-cost is at most Σ_i N_i r_i^(q+1)≤2Σ_i r_i^q<ε. The power cancellation r_i^(q+1)/r_i=r_i^q is valid because r_i>0. Rearranging these nonnegative sums is legitimate, and the upper bound is finite.

argument.text: F003 holds for arbitrary positive δ,ε. Discharge L2 to obtain existence of the stated arbitrarily fine arbitrarily cheap covers. This proves the output proposition on the whole asserted domain without any positive-diameter assumption on the covering sets.

argument.text: Fix X,A,s,δ and assume L1: s>0 and δ>0. Set c=C^s_δ(A), possibly ∞. Take any sequence V and assume L2: V is a δ-cover of A×I in MaxProd(X). Put ρ_i=diam(V_i), A_i=π_X(V_i), B_i=π_ℝ(V_i). Every V_i is bounded, since its extended diameter is ≤δ<∞. Each projection has pairwise distances at most ρ_i, whence diam A_i≤ρ_i and diam B_i≤ρ_i≤δ. For a nonempty V_i, B_i is nonempty and bounded above and below: choose any one of its points and use the finite diameter bound. Thus inf B_i and sup B_i exist as real numbers. Put J_i=[inf B_i,sup B_i]. The least-upper-bound and greatest-lower-bound properties give B_i⊆J_i and sup B_i-inf B_i≤ρ_i: for every b,b'∈B_i one has b-b'≤ρ_i, and taking supremum in b then infimum in b' preserves the inequality. In particular inf B_i≤sup B_i. For empty V_i put ρ_i=0 and A_i=B_i=J_i=∅. Each J_i is a closed real interval or ∅, hence Borel measurable, and all projection bounds remain valid. This construction imposes no measurability on V_i or its projections.

argument.text: For each nonempty member, apply M009 with endpoints inf B_i and sup B_i. By F001, volume(J_i)=ofReal(sup B_i-inf B_i)≤ρ_i. For an empty member volume(J_i)=volume(∅)=0=ρ_i by the empty-set axiom of a measure. Also I=[0,1] is closed and measurable and M009 with endpoints 0,1 gives volume(I)=1. Since I∩J_i⊆J_i, measure monotonicity gives volume(I∩J_i)≤volume(J_i)≤ρ_i; each intersection is measurable as an intersection of closed measurable sets.

argument.text: Define g(t)=1_I(t)c and f_seq(i)(t)=1_{I∩J_i}(t)ρ_i^s. Fix any real t. Universal introduction in t gives g≤Σ_i f_seq(i) pointwise on ℝ, also if c=∞. F002 shows that every indicator summand is Borel measurable: its only values are a nonnegative constant and zero on complementary measurable pieces, hence it is also volume-almost-everywhere measurable. Integrate F003 over ℝ with Lebesgue measure. M011 gives lintegral(volume,g)≤lintegral(volume,Σ_i f_seq(i)). M012 for I and constant c, together with volume(I)=1 from F002, gives lintegral(volume,g)=c·1=c, even when c=∞. M010 for the countable family f_seq exchanges the nonnegative series and lower integral, since F003 established almost-everywhere measurability of each summand. c=c·volume(I)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s volume(I∩J_i)

Each ρ_i is finite and nonnegative, and ρ_i^s·ρ_i=ρ_i^(s+1) holds for positive ρ_i by the real-power law and for ρ_i=0 because s>0. argument.text: Define e_h=e_basis(h) by the standard coordinate formula: its h-th coordinate is 1 and every other coordinate is 0. The n₀ coordinate unit vectors form a real basis of Rn(n₀): every vector is its finite coordinate linear combination, and equality of coordinates forces all coefficients in a zero combination to vanish. There are n₀ vectors. For n₀=0 this is the empty basis of the zero vector space. In MaxProd(Rn(n₀)), the n₀ vectors (e_h,0) together with (0,1) similarly span uniquely, by the first coordinates and last coordinate, so its real dimension is n₀+1. Both are real normed vector spaces (the second with the maximum product norm) and finite dimensional. Apply M007 to their full spaces and M006 to E⊆univ Rn(n₀) and F⊆univ MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). We obtain 0≤D≤n₀ and 0≤T≤n₀+1. The lower zero bounds follow from the ℝ≥0∞ codomain of dimH. Thus D and T are finite, including when n₀=0. A finite extended nonnegative real is the cast of its unique nonnegative real representative, and casts preserve finite sums and order.

produces.statement: 0≤D≤n₀<∞ and 0≤T≤n₀+1<∞; both dimensions have nonnegative real representatives with the same finite order and addition.

argument.text: The real line has basis {1}, hence real dimension one. The set I=[0,1] contains the open interval (0,1) in its interior: for each of its points the distance to the two endpoints has a positive minimum, giving a contained open ball. Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
\(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.

Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.

Basis proof for the complete selected target. All Hausdorff measures below are unnormalized diameter measures: no dimensional prefactor, ball-radius convention, probability normalization, or new hypothesis is introduced. The only H is the original one: n is an arbitrary natural number and E⊆Euclidean ℝ^n is nonempty and compact. Write X=Rn(n), I=[0,1], F=E×I, and D=dim_H E. We use the maximum metric on X×ℝ during the covering argument and return to the required Euclidean metric in paragraph 8. The original proof route is replaced only as recorded in the replacements array. The B statements are dependencies with proofs/reductions, not a permission list restricting the freely available pinned Mathlib.

1. Content and normalization (B101 from B001). For a>0 and δ>0 let C^a_δ(A) be the infimum of Σ_i(diam U_i)^a over countable δ-covers of A. In Lean this is BasisObjects.content a (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A. A set with extended diameter ≤δ<∞ is bounded, and its extended diameter is the cast of its real diameter. Empty sets contribute zero: the header explicitly uses the supremum over a nonemptiness proof, which is zero when empty and is the unique displayed value when nonempty. This also agrees with 0^a=0 for a>0. A finite cover may be padded by empty sets. A cover with any countable index type can be enumerated with empty padding after an injection into ℕ, and conversely an ℕ-family is countable. The sums are unchanged. Thus these contents coincide exactly with those in the original problem. No normalizing constant occurs.

The admissible covers for δ₁≤δ₂ form nested families, giving C^a_δ₂≤C^a_δ₁. Each admissible cover bounds the infimum above. A bound from below for every admissible cover bounds its infimum below, also when there are no admissible covers (infimum of the empty family is ∞). B001 identifies H^a with the supremum of these contents over positive extended scales. Scales ∞ add nothing: content at ∞ is at most the content at any fixed finite positive scale. Every finite positive extended scale is the cast of a positive real scale. Hence H^a(A)=sup_{δ>0} C^a_δ(A), exactly the problem's convention. In particular every finite-scale content is ≤H^a.

2. Approximation of a zero content (completion of B101). In the complete lattice ℝ≥0∞, if the infimum of a family is zero then for every finite ε>0 some family member is <ε; otherwise ε is a positive lower bound. Apply this to the nested infima over U and the cover and diameter conditions. An unsuccessful condition has empty infimum and value ∞, so a value <ε provides an actual admissible U. Conversely covers of arbitrarily small positive cost make the content zero. Taking the supremum over δ proves: H^a(A)=0 iff at every positive scale there are countable covers of arbitrarily small positive a-cost. All costs and sums are interpreted in ℝ≥0∞; finite estimates can equivalently be written in nonnegative reals.

3. Upper cover construction (B102). Let X be any metric space, A⊆X, q>0 and H^q(A)=0. Fix a target scale δ>0 and ε>0. Put r=min(1,δ)>0. By paragraph 2 choose a countable r-cover U_i with Σ d_i^q<ε/4, where d_i=diam U_i (zero for empty sets). Choose numbers 0<a_i≤r with a_i^q≤ε 2^(-i-3). For example take the minimum of r and (ε 2^(-i-3))^(1/q); all quantities are positive. Then Σ a_i^q≤ε/4, since Σ_{i≥0}2^(-i-3)=1/4. Put r_i=max(d_i,a_i). These numbers satisfy 0<r_i≤r≤1, and r_i^q=max(d_i^q,a_i^q)≤d_i^q+a_i^q. Summing gives Σ r_i^q<ε/2. This numerical padding handles zero-diameter singletons in every metric space, including X=ℝ^0; no replacement ball or additional ambient point is required.

Let N_i=ceil(1/r_i), a positive integer. The intervals [j/N_i,(j+1)/N_i], 0≤j<N_i, cover I and have length 1/N_i≤r_i. Also N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i. The products U_i×[j/N_i,(j+1)/N_i] cover A×I. Their diameters in the maximum metric are at most r_i, because both coordinate distances are at most r_i. Empty products have cost zero. The index set {(i,j):i∈ℕ, j<N_i} is countable, so this is an admissible countable cover at scale δ. Its total (q+1)-cost is at most Σ_i N_i r_i^(q+1)≤2 Σ_i r_i^q<ε. The equality r_i^(q+1)/r_i=r_i^q is legitimate since every r_i>0. As δ and ε were arbitrary, paragraph 2 gives H^(q+1)(A×I)=0.

4. Lower slicing construction (B103). Let X be any metric space, A⊆X, s>0 and δ>0. Set c=C^s_δ(A), with c allowed to be ∞. Take any countable δ-cover V_i of A×I in the maximum product metric. For a nonempty V_i let ρ_i=diam V_i, A_i=π_X(V_i), and B_i=π_ℝ(V_i). Coordinate distances do not exceed product distances, so diam A_i≤ρ_i≤δ and diam B_i≤ρ_i. A nonempty B_i is bounded above and below, because it has finite diameter; define J_i=[inf B_i,sup B_i]. The defining least-upper-bound and greatest-lower-bound inequalities show B_i⊆J_i. They also show sup B_i-inf B_i≤ρ_i: every b-b' with b,b'∈B_i is ≤ρ_i, then take the supremum in b and infimum in b'. Consequently J_i is a measurable closed interval and B007 gives volume J_i≤ρ_i. For empty V_i put ρ_i=0, A_i=B_i=J_i=∅; all these conclusions still hold. Notice that this does not assert measurability of V_i, A_i or B_i.

For any t∈I, the family consisting of A_i when t∈J_i and ∅ otherwise is a δ-cover of A. Indeed (x,t) lies in some V_i whenever x∈A, and then x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. Therefore
c≤Σ_i ρ_i^s 1_{J_i}(t) for every t∈I.
Equivalently, on all of ℝ,
1_I(t)c ≤ Σ_i 1_{I∩J_i}(t)ρ_i^s.
Outside I both sides are zero; this also works for c=∞ because indicator functions use a zero branch, avoiding any ambiguous real multiplication. Every I∩J_i is measurable. Integrate this inequality with Lebesgue measure. B009 gives monotonicity, B010 evaluates the indicators, B007 gives volume I=1, and B008 exchanges the nonnegative series and lower integral. The result is
c=c·volume I
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s volume(I∩J_i)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s volume J_i
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s ρ_i
 =Σ_i ρ_i^(s+1).
Indicator summands are measurable, hence AEMeasurable as required by B008. The second inequality uses inclusion and the monotonicity of a measure. All powers are nonnegative; ρ_i is finite; the power identity holds also for ρ_i=0 because s>0. These inequalities hold in ℝ≥0∞, and do not require c or the series to be finite. Taking the infimum over the arbitrary covers gives C^s_δ(A)≤C^(s+1)_δ(A×I). Taking suprema over δ and using paragraph 1 gives H^s(A)≤H^(s+1)(A×I).

5. Finite dimensions and the fibre bound (part of B104). By B003 and B004,
0≤D≤dimH(X)=finrank ℝ X=n.
The rank equality follows from the n standard Euclidean coordinate vectors; for n=0 it is the empty basis. Thus D is finite and may be identified with its nonnegative real value without changing addition or order. The same argument in X×ℝ gives dimH F≤n+1<∞ in the maximum norm; its coordinate basis has n+1 vectors.

The set I has nonempty real interior: (0,1)⊆interior I and, for example, 1/2 belongs to it. B012 with finrank ℝ ℝ=1 gives dimH I=1. Choose x₀∈E using the original nonemptiness assumption. The map t↦(x₀,t) is an isometry for the maximum product metric, since max(dist(x₀,x₀),|t-u|)=|t-u|. B006 and B003 therefore give dimH F≥dimH({x₀}×I)=1. This also proves the entire required lower bound when D=0.

6. Upper dimension inequality (part of B104). For any real q>D, we have q>0. Regard q as a nonnegative real when invoking B002. Its critical-exponent zero conclusion gives H^q(E)=0. Paragraph 3 gives H^(q+1)(F)=0, so this measure is not ∞ and B002 gives dimH F≤q+1. This holds for every q>D. Because D and dimH F are finite, it implies dimH F≤D+1: if dimH F>D+1, choose q strictly between D and dimH F-1, contradicting dimH F≤q+1. No assumption n≥1 has been made, so this includes n=0.

7. Lower dimension inequality (completion of B104). If D>0, choose any real s with 0<s<D. B002 gives H^s(E)=∞. Paragraph 4 gives H^(s+1)(F)≥H^s(E)=∞, so H^(s+1)(F)=∞. B002 now yields dimH F≥s+1. Together with the fibre bound this implies dimH F≥D+1: if instead dimH F<D+1, the fibre bound gives dimH F-1≥0, and one can choose s strictly between dimH F-1 and D, a contradiction. If D=0, paragraph 5 already gives dimH F≥D+1. Combined with paragraph 6 this proves the maximum-norm equality for every n and the original nonempty compact E. Compactness is retained as H even though the replacement cover argument needs no further use of it.

8. Return to the specified Euclidean target (B105). The header defines euclideanLift n as the identity on pairs into WithLp 2 (Rn(n)×ℝ). The prepared adapter B011 is an actual closed Lean proof from B005 using the inverse of WithLp.prodContinuousLinearEquiv 2 ℝ (Rn n) ℝ. Its underlying function is exactly euclideanLift, and it proves that every image set has the same Hausdorff dimension as in the maximum norm. This is an explicit metric-change justification, valid for all n≥0 and all sets.

B013 shows that the norm in this new space satisfies ‖(x,t)‖²=‖x‖²+|t|². Apply it to differences. In Rn(n), the squared Euclidean norm is Σ_{j<n}|x_j|² by the defining Euclidean norm. Consequently coordinate concatenation j(x,t)=(x₀,…,x_(n-1),t) has
dist(j(x,t),j(y,u))²=Σ_{j<n}|x_j-y_j|²+|t-u|²
=dist(euclideanLift(x,t),euclideanLift(y,u))².
Distances are nonnegative, so equality of squares gives equality of distances. This proves an isometry into Euclidean ℝ^(n+1); truncation of the first n coordinates and extraction of the last coordinate give its inverse. For n=0 the sum is empty and the same construction is the usual identification of ℝ^0×ℝ with ℝ. It sends euclideanLift '' (E×I) exactly to the original Euclidean product set. B006 preserves its dimension. Applying B011 and paragraph 7 therefore gives, in precisely the selected Euclidean metric,
dim_H(E×[0,1])=dim_H E+1.
The right side is the original dimension of E in the Euclidean metric of ℝ^n. All dimensions here are finite, so the ℝ≥0∞ equality is the same equality of real dimensions in the original statement. This completes the full target without residual textbook premises.

import Mathlib
open scoped ENNReal NNReal Topology
open Set MeasureTheory
namespace BasisObjects
abbrev Rn (n : ℕ) := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)
noncomputable def content {X : Type*} [EMetricSpace X]
    (s : ℝ) (r : ℝ≥0∞) (A : Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨅ (U : ℕ → Set X) (_ : A ⊆ ⋃ i, U i)
    (_ : ∀ i, Metric.ediam (U i) ≤ r),
      ∑' i, ⨆ (_ : (U i).Nonempty), (Metric.ediam (U i)) ^ s
def euclideanLift (n : ℕ) : Rn n × ℝ → WithLp 2 (Rn n × ℝ) :=
  WithLp.toLp 2

Every cost bounds its infimum above; a lower bound on every admissible cost bounds the infimum below. If the admissible family is empty its infimum is ∞, and the latter assertion remains true. For any positive extended scale r, if it is finite it is the cast of a positive real scale. We have proved H^a(A)=sup_{δ>0}C^a_δ(A), and each such content is ≤H^a(A).

Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
\(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.

Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.

value.statement: For every metric space X, subset A⊆X and real a>0, the positive-scale contents C^a_δ(A) are exactly the unnormalized real-diameter countable-cover contents of the original problem. argument.text: Fix X,A,a and assume L1: a>0. Work with X's Borel structure, so M001 applies and gives H^a(A)=sup_{r>0} content(a,r,A) over extended nonnegative r. For arbitrary δ, temporarily assume L2: δ>0. At the finite scale ofReal δ, every admissible covering member has finite extended diameter, hence is bounded and has ediam equal to its real diameter cast to ℝ≥0∞. The nonemptiness-proof supremum in D004 is the displayed diameter power on a nonempty member and is zero on an empty member. For a>0 this agrees with assigning the empty member diameter zero and 0^a=0. Thus the nested infima are exactly the original admissible-cover infimum, with no prefactor. A finite family can be padded by empty sets. For an arbitrary countable index type choose an injection into ℕ; at each image index put the unique original member and elsewhere put ∅. This preserves the union and all nonnegative sums. Conversely an ℕ-family is countable. Discharge L2 after this finite-scale interpretation, retaining its δ>0 antecedent for every δ. For arbitrary δ₁,δ₂, temporarily assume L3: 0<δ₁≤δ₂. Every δ₁-cover is a δ₂-cover, so C^a_δ₂(A)≤C^a_δ₁(A). Discharge L3 and quantify the two scales. Every cost bounds its infimum above; a lower bound on every admissible cost bounds the infimum below. If the admissible family is empty its infimum is ∞, and the latter assertion remains true. For any positive extended scale r, if it is finite it is the cast of a positive real scale. The content at r=∞ is at most that at any fixed finite positive scale, since every finite-scale cover is also an ∞-cover. Hence the ∞ scale adds nothing to the supremum. We have proved H^a(A)=sup_{δ>0}C^a_δ(A), and each such content is ≤H^a(A).

produces.statement: Under a>0, the contents have the real-diameter countable-cover interpretation with empty padding/reindexing; they are nonincreasing in positive scale, satisfy the two infimum bounds, and H^a(A)=sup_{δ_bound>0}C^a_{δ_bound}(A).

argument.text: For the arbitrary δ,ε, temporarily assume L4: δ>0 and ε>0. Suppose L5: C^a_δ(A)=0. if every admissible cost were ≥ε, the lower-bound property in F001 would imply C^a_δ(A)≥ε>0, a contradiction. Thus an admissible cover of cost <ε exists. Discharge L5 to obtain the forward implication. In terms of the nested infima in D004, any failed cover or diameter condition has value ∞ and cannot give a value <ε, so the approximation provides an actual admissible family. Conversely assume L6: for every positive tolerance there exists an admissible cover of smaller cost. This forces the nonnegative content to be zero: a positive value, finite or infinite, has some positive finite real below it, contradicting the upper bound by those costs. Discharge L6, then L4, and quantify the arbitrary positive scale and tolerance. This proves the zero-content approximation equivalence for every positive scale. These arguments also cover an empty admissible family, whose content is ∞.

produces.statement: For every δ_bound>0, C^a_{δ_bound}(A)=0 iff at every positive finite real tolerance there exists an admissible countable δ_bound-cover of A of smaller a-cost.

argument.text: By F001, H^a(A)=0 implies each positive-scale content is zero; F002 then gives the required arbitrarily small covers at every scale. Conversely, those covers make every positive-scale content zero by F002, and their supremum is zero by F001. This proves the full equivalence and all asserted content properties. Discharge L1 to retain a>0 as an antecedent and universally quantify X,A,a and the scale/tolerance variables. No boundedness or measurability assumption on A is used.

applications.bindings: Take W=X with its Borel structure, exponent a and set A; expand the extended-scale content exactly as D004.
hypothesis_checks: The fixed X is a metric space, hence an emetric space, and we explicitly chose its Borel measurable structure.

locals.type: metric space with its Borel structure
locals.declaration: Fix an arbitrary metric space X.
Fix A⊆X.
Fix real q, under L1: q>0 and H^q(A)=0.
Fix a target scale δ, with its positivity in L2.
Fix a tolerance ε, with its positivity in L2.
Put r=min(1,δ).
Choose the admissible r-cover U supplied by F001, with Σ diam(U_i)^q<ε/4.
Set d_i=diam(U_i), which is defined since U is a finite-scale cover.
Set r_seq(i)=max(d_i,a_seq(i)). Write r_i for r_seq(i).
For each natural i put N_seq(i)=ceil(1/r_seq(i)); write N_i for this integer.

locals.type: countable family of subsets of MaxProd(X)
locals.declaration: For natural i and 0≤h<N_seq(i), set W_seq(i,h)=U_i×[h/N_seq(i),(h+1)/N_seq(i)].

argument.text: Fix X,A,q and assume L1: q>0 and H^q(A)=0. Fix arbitrary real δ,ε and assume L2: δ>0 and ε>0. Put r=min(1,δ), so 0<r≤1 and r≤δ. By N001 with exponent q, scale r and tolerance ε/4 there exists a countable r-cover U of A whose total q-cost is <ε/4; reindex it as a sequence with empty padding if necessary. In particular its members have finite diameter.

produces.statement: There exists a sequence U_bound of subsets of X covering A such that diam(U_bound(i))≤r for every natural i and Σ_i diam(U_bound(i))^q<ε/4.

argument.text: Choose U from F001 and put d_i=diam(U_i), with d_i=0 on empty members. For each natural i define a_seq(i)=min(r,(ε·2^(-i-3))^(1/q)). Both entries of this minimum are positive, so 0<a_seq(i)≤r and a_seq(i)^q≤ε·2^(-i-3). The nonnegative geometric series has sum Σ_{i≥0}2^(-i-3)=1/4 (its partial sums are (1/4)(1-2^(-m)) for the first m terms). Hence Σ a_seq(i)^q≤ε/4. Put r_i=max(d_i,a_seq(i)). Then 0<r_i≤r≤1 and r_i^q=max(d_i^q,a_seq(i)^q)≤d_i^q+a_seq(i)^q. Summing nonnegative terms, using F001 and the geometric bound, gives Σ r_i^q<ε/2. Numerical padding changes no covering set and works even if X is a singleton.

produces.statement: U covers A, d_i=diam(U_i)≤r_i, and 0<r_i≤r≤min(1,δ) for all natural i; Σ_i r_i^q<ε/2.

argument.text: For each natural i put N_i=ceil(1/r_i), a positive integer. Then 1/N_i≤r_i and N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i, since 0<r_i≤1. The closed intervals [h/N_i,(h+1)/N_i], 0≤h<N_i, cover I. Define W_seq(i,h)=U_i×[h/N_i,(h+1)/N_i]. In the maximum product metric any two points of this product have distance at most r_i, since the first-coordinate diameter is d_i≤r_i and the second-coordinate interval length is 1/N_i≤r_i. The product family covers A×I, and its index set {(i,h):i∈ℕ,0≤h<N_i} is countable. Empty products have zero cost. By N001 this countable family may be reindexed into ℕ without changing the union or sum. It is a δ-cover, and its total (q+1)-cost is at most Σ_i N_i r_i^(q+1)≤2Σ_i r_i^q<ε. The power cancellation r_i^(q+1)/r_i=r_i^q is valid because r_i>0. Rearranging these nonnegative sums is legitimate, and the upper bound is finite.

produces.statement: There exists a countable δ-cover of A×I in MaxProd(X) with total (q+1)-cost <ε.

argument.text: F003 holds for arbitrary positive δ,ε. Discharge L2 to obtain existence of the stated arbitrarily fine arbitrarily cheap covers. Since q+1>0, N001, now for MaxProd(X), A×I and exponent q+1, implies H^(q+1)(A×I)=0. Discharge L1 and universally quantify X,A,q. This proves the output proposition on the whole asserted domain without any positive-diameter assumption on the covering sets.

locals.type: metric space with its Borel structure
locals.declaration: Fix an arbitrary metric space X.
Fix any A⊆X.
Fix real s with positivity in L1.
Fix real scale δ with positivity in L1.
Set c=C^s_δ(A), allowing c=∞.
Take any sequence V; under L2 assume it covers A×I and has each diameter ≤δ.
Write ρ_i=rho(i)=diam(V_i), with value zero on empty members.
A_seq(i)=π_X(V_i), written A_i.
B_seq(i)=π_ℝ(V_i), written B_i.
Put J_i=[inf B_i,sup B_i] for nonempty V_i and J_i=∅ for empty V_i. The infimum/supremum are of bounded nonempty sets, as proved in S001.
Set f_seq(i)(t)=1_{I∩J_seq(i)}(t) rho(i)^s.
Set g(t)=1_I(t)c, with the zero indicator branch outside I.
Fix an arbitrary real t in the pointwise proof.
For the coverage verification fix any x∈X; membership in A is the temporary antecedent L4.

argument.text: Fix X,A,s,δ and assume L1: s>0 and δ>0. Set c=C^s_δ(A), possibly ∞. Take any sequence V and assume L2: V is a δ-cover of A×I in MaxProd(X). Put ρ_i=diam(V_i), A_i=π_X(V_i), B_i=π_ℝ(V_i). Every V_i is bounded, since its extended diameter is ≤δ<∞. Each projection has pairwise distances at most ρ_i, whence diam A_i≤ρ_i and diam B_i≤ρ_i≤δ. For a nonempty V_i, B_i is nonempty and bounded above and below: choose any one of its points and use the finite diameter bound. Thus inf B_i and sup B_i exist as real numbers. Put J_i=[inf B_i,sup B_i]. The least-upper-bound and greatest-lower-bound properties give B_i⊆J_i and sup B_i-inf B_i≤ρ_i: for every b,b'∈B_i one has b-b'≤ρ_i, and taking supremum in b then infimum in b' preserves the inequality. In particular inf B_i≤sup B_i. For empty V_i put ρ_i=0 and A_i=B_i=J_i=∅. Each J_i is a closed real interval or ∅, hence Borel measurable, and all projection bounds remain valid. This construction imposes no measurability on V_i or its projections.

produces.statement: For every natural i, A_i=π_X(V_i), B_i=π_ℝ(V_i), B_i⊆J_i, diam(A_i)≤ρ_i≤δ, and J_i is Borel measurable; for nonempty V_i it is [inf B_i,sup B_i] with 0≤sup B_i-inf B_i≤ρ_i, and for empty V_i all these sets are empty and ρ_i=0.

argument.text: For each nonempty member, apply M009 with endpoints inf B_i and sup B_i. By F001, volume(J_i)=ofReal(sup B_i-inf B_i)≤ρ_i. For an empty member volume(J_i)=volume(∅)=0=ρ_i by the empty-set axiom of a measure. Also I=[0,1] is closed and measurable and M009 with endpoints 0,1 gives volume(I)=1. Since I∩J_i⊆J_i, measure monotonicity gives volume(I∩J_i)≤volume(J_i)≤ρ_i; each intersection is measurable as an intersection of closed measurable sets.

produces.statement: I and every I∩J_i are Borel measurable, volume(I)=1, and volume(I∩J_i)≤volume(J_i)≤ρ_i for every natural i.

argument.text: Define g(t)=1_I(t)c and f_seq(i)(t)=1_{I∩J_i}(t)ρ_i^s. Fix any real t. In the case L3: t∈I, the family consisting of A_i when t∈J_i and ∅ otherwise covers A: under the auxiliary antecedent L4: x∈A, L2 supplies an i with (x,t)∈V_i, so x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. This proves membership in the projected union; discharge L4 and quantify x. Each such projected set has diameter ≤ρ_i≤δ by F001. N001 therefore gives c≤Σ_i ρ_i^s 1_{J_i}(t)=Σ_i f_seq(i)(t). Discharge L3 after the inside-I argument. If t∉I, g(t)=0 and every f_seq(i)(t)=0 by the indicator zero branch, so the same inequality holds. Universal introduction in t gives g≤Σ_i f_seq(i) pointwise on ℝ, also if c=∞. F002 shows that every indicator summand is Borel measurable: its only values are a nonnegative constant and zero on complementary measurable pieces, hence it is also volume-almost-everywhere measurable. No product of an undefined infinite real quantity is used.

produces.statement: g≤(t↦Σ_i f_seq(i)(t)) pointwise on ℝ, and every f_seq(i) is volume-almost-everywhere measurable, with g=1_I c and f_seq(i)=1_{I∩J_i}ρ_i^s.

argument.text:
Integrate F003 over ℝ with Lebesgue measure. M011 gives lintegral(volume,g)≤lintegral(volume,Σ_i f_seq(i)). M012 for I and constant c, together with volume(I)=1 from F002, gives lintegral(volume,g)=c·1=c, even when c=∞. M010 for the countable family f_seq exchanges the nonnegative series and lower integral, since F003 established almost-everywhere measurability of each summand. M012 for I∩J_i and constant ρ_i^s evaluates each term. Thus
c=c·volume(I)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s volume(I∩J_i)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s volume(J_i)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s ρ_i
 =Σ_i ρ_i^(s+1).
The middle bounds use F002 and monotonicity of multiplication and nonnegative sums. Each ρ_i is finite and nonnegative, and ρ_i^s·ρ_i=ρ_i^(s+1) holds for positive ρ_i by the real-power law and for ρ_i=0 because s>0. This is an ℝ≥0∞ computation; neither c nor the series need be finite. Discharge L2: every admissible δ-cover has (s+1)-cost at least c.

produces.statement: Every admissible countable δ-cover of A×I in MaxProd(X) has total (s+1)-cost at least c=C^s_δ(A).

argument.text: By the lower-infimum bound in N001, F004 implies C^s_δ(A)≤C^(s+1)_δ(A×I), including if no admissible product cover exists. This holds at every δ>0. Taking suprema over positive scales and using N001 for both positive exponents s and s+1 gives H^s(A)≤H^(s+1)(A×I). Discharge L1 and universally quantify X,A,s and the scale. These are the complete scale and measure inequalities asserted in the output proposition.

applications.bindings: For each nonempty V_i set a=inf B_i,b=sup B_i; also set a=0,b=1 for I.
Take W=ℝ with its Borel structure, μ=volume, f=g and the source upper function equal to t↦Σ_i f_seq(i)(t).
hypothesis_checks: ℝ is a measurable Borel space and volume is Lebesgue measure.
F003 proves this pointwise inequality on all of ℝ, including outside I.

applications.bindings: Take W=ℝ, μ=volume, J=ℕ, and the source family f=f_seq.
hypothesis_checks: ℝ has its Borel measurable structure and volume is a measure.
ℕ is countable.
F003 proves each f_seq(i) measurable, hence volume-almost-everywhere measurable.

applications.bindings: Take W=ℝ, μ=volume, B=I and constant c=C^s_δ(A).
hypothesis_checks: ℝ with its Borel structure and Lebesgue volume is a measured space.
F002 states that I is measurable.

applications.bindings: For every natural i take W=ℝ, μ=volume, B=I∩J_i and the nonnegative constant ρ_i^s.
hypothesis_checks: ℝ with its Borel structure and Lebesgue volume is a measured space.
F002 states that every I∩J_i is measurable.

locals.type: family of vectors of Rn(n₀) indexed by h<n₀
locals.declaration: Define e_basis(h), written e_h, to have coordinate 1 at h and 0 at every other coordinate.
Choose x_f∈E by H001.
Define f_f(t)=(x_f,t).
In the distance-preservation calculation fix arbitrary real t.
In the distance-preservation calculation fix arbitrary real u.

argument.text: Define e_h=e_basis(h) by the standard coordinate formula: its h-th coordinate is 1 and every other coordinate is 0. The n₀ coordinate unit vectors form a real basis of Rn(n₀): every vector is its finite coordinate linear combination, and equality of coordinates forces all coefficients in a zero combination to vanish. There are n₀ vectors. For n₀=0 this is the empty basis of the zero vector space. In MaxProd(Rn(n₀)), the n₀ vectors (e_h,0) together with (0,1) similarly span uniquely, by the first coordinates and last coordinate, so its real dimension is n₀+1. Both are real normed vector spaces (the second with the maximum product norm) and finite dimensional. Apply M007 to their full spaces and M006 to E⊆univ Rn(n₀) and F⊆univ MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). We obtain 0≤D≤n₀ and 0≤T≤n₀+1. The lower zero bounds follow from the ℝ≥0∞ codomain of dimH. Thus D and T are finite, including when n₀=0. A finite extended nonnegative real is the cast of its unique nonnegative real representative, and casts preserve finite sums and order.

produces.statement: 0≤D≤n₀<∞ and 0≤T≤n₀+1<∞; both dimensions have nonnegative real representatives with the same finite order and addition.

argument.text: The real line has basis {1}, hence real dimension one. The set I=[0,1] contains the open interval (0,1) in its interior: for each of its points the distance to the two endpoints has a positive minimum, giving a contained open ball. In particular 1/2 belongs to the interior. Apply M013 to the real normed space ℝ and A=I. Its hypotheses hold and it gives dimH(I)=1.

produces.statement: dimH(I)=1.

argument.text: H001 supplies x_f∈E. Define f_f(t)=(x_f,t). For any real t,u, the maximum product distance between f_f(t) and f_f(u) is max(dist(x_f,x_f),|t-u|)=|t-u|. Thus f_f is an isometry; its image of I is {x_f}×I, a subset of F by x_f∈E.

produces.statement: f_f:ℝ→MaxProd(Rn(n₀)) is an isometry and f_f '' I⊆F.

argument.text: Apply M008 to f_f and I, using the isometry in F003. It gives dimH(f_f '' I)=dimH(I)=1 by F002. Apply M006 to f_f '' I⊆F, also in F003, to get 1≤dimH(F)=T. Combining with F001 proves 0≤D≤n₀<∞ and 1≤T≤n₀+1<∞, together with dimH(I)=1 and the finite real identifications. The chosen point and its map do not occur in the output proposition.

applications.bindings: Take W=Rn(n₀), then W=MaxProd(Rn(n₀)).
hypothesis_checks: Both are real normed vector spaces by D001 and D009.
S001 displays bases of size n₀ and n₀+1, including the empty basis for Rn(0).

applications.bindings: Take W=Rn(n₀), A=E,B=univ; then W=MaxProd(Rn(n₀)), A=F,B=univ.
hypothesis_checks: Each normed space is a metric, hence emetric space.
Every set is contained in its full ambient space.

applications.bindings: Take W=ℝ and A=I.
hypothesis_checks: ℝ has its usual real normed vector-space structure.
The singleton basis {1} spans ℝ and is linearly independent.
S002 proves (0,1)⊆interior I and exhibits the point 1/2.

applications.bindings: Take W=ℝ, Z=MaxProd(Rn(n₀)), f=f_f and A=I.
hypothesis_checks: The real line and the maximum product are metric, hence emetric spaces.
F003 proves distance preservation; finite real distances give extended distance preservation as well.

applications.bindings: Take W=MaxProd(Rn(n₀)), A=f_f '' I and B=F.
hypothesis_checks: The maximum product is a metric, hence emetric space.
F003 exports the required image inclusion.

locals.declaration: Let d_real be the finite real representative of D from N004.
Let k_real be the finite real representative of T from N004.
Fix arbitrary real q; the condition q>d_real is the local antecedent L1.
Under L2 put q_mid=(d_real+k_real-1)/2.

argument.text: By N004, write D and T as casts of finite real values d_real≥0 and k_real≥1, respectively. Order and addition of these finite values agree with their real operations.

produces.statement: D is the cast of d_real≥0, T is the cast of k_real≥1, and the casts preserve their finite order and addition.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary real q and assume L1: q>d_real. F001 gives q>0, so q defines a nonnegative real exponent. M003 with set E and exponent q gives H^q(E)=0, since dimH(E)=D<q. Apply N002 to X=Rn(n₀), A=E and q. Its positive-exponent and zero-measure premises have just been established, and E×I in MaxProd(Rn(n₀)) is F. Therefore H^(q+1)(F)=0.

Since q+1>0, it is also a nonnegative real exponent. By F002 its Hausdorff measure on F is zero, hence different from ∞. Apply M004 with F and exponent q+1. It gives T≤q+1, equivalently k_real≤q+1 by F001. Discharge L1: for every real q>d_real one has k_real≤q+1.

produces.statement: For every real q_bound>d_real, k_real≤q_bound+1.

argument.text: Assume for contradiction L2: k_real>d_real+1. Put q_mid=(d_real+k_real-1)/2. Then d_real<q_mid<k_real-1, because k_real-1>d_real. F003 with q=q_mid gives k_real≤q_mid+1<k_real, a contradiction. Discharge L2 to obtain k_real≤d_real+1. Cast back by F001: T≤D+1. Finiteness is already supplied by F001. This proves the output proposition for every natural n₀, including zero.

applications.bindings: Take W=Rn(n₀) with its Borel structure, A=E and source nonnegative exponent d equal to q.
hypothesis_checks: Rn(n₀) is a Euclidean metric space and is equipped with its Borel structure.
F001 and L1 give q>d_real≥0.
D=dimH(E) is the cast of d_real by F001, so L1 gives dimH(E)<q.

applications.bindings: Take W=MaxProd(Rn(n₀)) with its Borel structure, A=F and source exponent d=q+1.
hypothesis_checks: The maximum product is a metric space with its Borel structure.
F002 gives q>0, hence q+1>0.
F002 gives H^(q+1)(F)=0 and zero is different from ∞.

locals.declaration: Let d_real be the finite nonnegative real representative of D given by N004.
Let k_real be the finite real representative of T given by N004.
Under L1,L2 set s_mid=(k_real-1+d_real)/2.

argument.text: By N004 write D,T as casts of real values d_real≥0 and k_real≥1. Their orders and addition agree with real operations. If L3: d_real=0, the fibre bound k_real≥1 gives k_real≥d_real+1. Discharge L3 to retain this implication. Since d_real≥0, the other case is d_real>0.

produces.statement: D and T are the casts of d_real≥0 and k_real≥1 with compatible order and addition, and d_real=0 implies k_real≥d_real+1.

argument.text: Assume L1: d_real>0. To prove the lower bound, assume for contradiction L2: k_real<d_real+1. Then 0≤k_real-1<d_real by F001. Put s_mid=(k_real-1+d_real)/2. These inequalities imply 0<s_mid<d_real and k_real<s_mid+1. The strict positivity of s_mid follows from d_real>0 even if k_real-1=0.

produces.statement: 0<s_mid<d_real and k_real<s_mid+1.

argument.text: By F002, M002 applied to E at the nonnegative exponent s_mid gives H^s_mid(E)=∞, because dimH(E)=D is the cast of d_real. N003, applied with X=Rn(n₀), A=E and s=s_mid, gives H^s_mid(E)≤H^(s_mid+1)(F). Consequently H^(s_mid+1)(F)=∞.

M005 with A=F and the nonnegative exponent s_mid+1 yields s_mid+1≤T from F003, equivalently s_mid+1≤k_real by F001. This contradicts F002. Discharge L2 and conclude k_real≥d_real+1 under L1. Discharge L1, and combine with the d_real=0 implication in F001 by exhaustive cases on d_real≥0. Hence k_real≥d_real+1 for all cases.

produces.statement: k_real≥d_real+1, equivalently T≥D+1.

argument.text: F004 gives T≥D+1, and N005 gives T≤D+1. Antisymmetry proves T=D+1. Both dimensions and their sum are finite by F001 and N004. When n₀=0, N004 forces D=0 and the fibre branch already supplies the lower bound; the upper proof also covered this case. This proves the output proposition. Compactness remains an original hypothesis in the global specification, although this replacement proof does not use it.

applications.bindings: Take W=Rn(n₀) with its Borel structure, A=E, and the nonnegative exponent d=s_mid.
hypothesis_checks: Rn(n₀) is Euclidean and equipped with its Borel structure.
F002 establishes s_mid>0.
F001 identifies dimH(E)=D with d_real and F002 gives s_mid<d_real.

applications.bindings: Take W=MaxProd(Rn(n₀)) with its Borel structure, A=F and exponent d=s_mid+1.
hypothesis_checks: The maximum product is a metric space with its Borel structure.
F002 gives s_mid>0, hence s_mid+1≥0.
F003, proved in S003 from M002 and N003, states H^(s_mid+1)(F)=∞.

locals.declaration: Fix arbitrary p∈L2Prod(n₀).
Fix arbitrary z∈L2Prod(n₀).
For the inverse construction take any v∈Rn(n₀+1).
For the final squared-distance specialization fix arbitrary x of the declared type.
For the final squared-distance specialization fix arbitrary y of the declared type.
For the final squared-distance specialization fix arbitrary t of the declared type.
For the final squared-distance specialization fix arbitrary u of the declared type.

argument.text:
Fix arbitrary p,z∈L2Prod(n₀). Apply M014 with W=Rn(n₀), Z=ℝ and argument p-z. These are normed additive commutative groups, hence satisfy its seminormed assumptions. With the coordinatewise subtraction and distance as norm of difference, the source gives
 dist(p,z)²=‖p.fst-z.fst‖²+|p.snd-z.snd|²
 =Σ_{h<n₀}|p.fst_h-z.fst_h|²+|p.snd-z.snd|².
The second equality uses the defining squared Euclidean norm on Rn(n₀). On the other hand, the defining squared norm on Rn(n₀+1), split into its first n₀ coordinates and last coordinate, gives
 dist(j(n₀)(p),j(n₀)(z))²=Σ_{h<n₀}|p.fst_h-z.fst_h|²+|p.snd-z.snd|².
The two nonnegative distances have equal squares; hence they are equal. These formulas hold also when n₀=0, with an empty finite sum.

produces.statement: For all p_bound,z_bound∈L2Prod(n₀), dist(j(n₀)(p_bound),j(n₀)(z_bound))=dist(p_bound,z_bound), and their common square is Σ_{h<n₀}|p_bound.fst_h-z_bound.fst_h|²+|p_bound.snd-z_bound.snd|².

argument.text: By F001, j(n₀) is an isometry. Conversely the supremum bounds all pairwise distances and casts preserve the finite bound.

value.text: Fix X,A,a and assume L1: a>0. Work with X's Borel structure, so M001 applies and gives H^a(A)=sup_{r>0} content(a,r,A) over extended nonnegative r. For arbitrary δ, temporarily assume L2: δ>0. At the finite scale ofReal δ, every admissible covering member has finite extended diameter, hence is bounded and has ediam equal to its real diameter cast to ℝ≥0∞. The nonemptiness-proof supremum in D004 is the displayed diameter power on a nonempty member and is zero on an empty member. For a>0 this agrees with assigning the empty member diameter zero and 0^a=0. Thus the nested infima are exactly the original admissible-cover infimum, with no prefactor. A finite family can be padded by empty sets. For an arbitrary countable index type choose an injection into ℕ; at each image index put the unique original member and elsewhere put ∅. This preserves the union and all nonnegative sums. Conversely an ℕ-family is countable. Discharge L2 after this finite-scale interpretation, retaining its δ>0 antecedent for every δ. For arbitrary δ₁,δ₂, temporarily assume L3: 0<δ₁≤δ₂. Every δ₁-cover is a δ₂-cover, so C^a_δ₂(A)≤C^a_δ₁(A). Discharge L3 and quantify the two scales. Every cost bounds its infimum above; a lower bound on every admissible cost bounds the infimum below. If the admissible family is empty its infimum is ∞, and the latter assertion remains true. For any positive extended scale r, if it is finite it is the cast of a positive real scale. The content at r=∞ is at most that at any fixed finite positive scale, since every finite-scale cover is also an ∞-cover. Hence the ∞ scale adds nothing to the supremum. We have proved H^a(A)=sup_{δ>0}C^a_δ(A), and each such content is ≤H^a(A).

For the arbitrary δ,ε, temporarily assume L4: δ>0 and ε>0. Suppose L5: C^a_δ(A)=0. if every admissible cost were ≥ε, the lower-bound property in F001 would imply C^a_δ(A)≥ε>0, a contradiction. Thus an admissible cover of cost <ε exists. Discharge L5 to obtain the forward implication. In terms of the nested infima in D004, any failed cover or diameter condition has value ∞ and cannot give a value <ε, so the approximation provides an actual admissible family. Conversely assume L6: for every positive tolerance there exists an admissible cover of smaller cost. This forces the nonnegative content to be zero: a positive value, finite or infinite, has some positive finite real below it, contradicting the upper bound by those costs. Discharge L6, then L4, and quantify the arbitrary positive scale and tolerance. This proves the zero-content approximation equivalence for every positive scale. These arguments also cover an empty admissible family, whose content is ∞.

By F001, H^a(A)=0 implies each positive-scale content is zero; F002 then gives the required arbitrarily small covers at every scale. Conversely, those covers make every positive-scale content zero by F002, and their supremum is zero by F001. This proves the full equivalence and all asserted content properties. Discharge L1 to retain a>0 as an antecedent and universally quantify X,A,a and the scale/tolerance variables. No boundedness or measurability assumption on A is used.

Fix X,A,q and assume L1: q>0 and H^q(A)=0. Fix arbitrary real δ,ε and assume L2: δ>0 and ε>0. Put r=min(1,δ), so 0<r≤1 and r≤δ. By N001 with exponent q, scale r and tolerance ε/4 there exists a countable r-cover U of A whose total q-cost is <ε/4; reindex it as a sequence with empty padding if necessary. In particular its members have finite diameter.

Choose U from F001 and put d_i=diam(U_i), with d_i=0 on empty members. For each natural i define a_seq(i)=min(r,(ε·2^(-i-3))^(1/q)). Both entries of this minimum are positive, so 0<a_seq(i)≤r and a_seq(i)^q≤ε·2^(-i-3). The nonnegative geometric series has sum Σ_{i≥0}2^(-i-3)=1/4 (its partial sums are (1/4)(1-2^(-m)) for the first m terms). Hence Σ a_seq(i)^q≤ε/4. Put r_i=max(d_i,a_seq(i)). Then 0<r_i≤r≤1 and r_i^q=max(d_i^q,a_seq(i)^q)≤d_i^q+a_seq(i)^q. Summing nonnegative terms, using F001 and the geometric bound, gives Σ r_i^q<ε/2. Numerical padding changes no covering set and works even if X is a singleton.

For each natural i put N_i=ceil(1/r_i), a positive integer. Then 1/N_i≤r_i and N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i, since 0<r_i≤1. The closed intervals [h/N_i,(h+1)/N_i], 0≤h<N_i, cover I. Define W_seq(i,h)=U_i×[h/N_i,(h+1)/N_i]. In the maximum product metric any two points of this product have distance at most r_i, since the first-coordinate diameter is d_i≤r_i and the second-coordinate interval length is 1/N_i≤r_i. The product family covers A×I, and its index set {(i,h):i∈ℕ,0≤h<N_i} is countable. Empty products have zero cost. By N001 this countable family may be reindexed into ℕ without changing the union or sum. It is a δ-cover, and its total (q+1)-cost is at most Σ_i N_i r_i^(q+1)≤2Σ_i r_i^q<ε. The power cancellation r_i^(q+1)/r_i=r_i^q is valid because r_i>0. Rearranging these nonnegative sums is legitimate, and the upper bound is finite.

F003 holds for arbitrary positive δ,ε. Discharge L2 to obtain existence of the stated arbitrarily fine arbitrarily cheap covers. Since q+1>0, N001, now for MaxProd(X), A×I and exponent q+1, implies H^(q+1)(A×I)=0. Discharge L1 and universally quantify X,A,q. This proves the output proposition on the whole asserted domain without any positive-diameter assumption on the covering sets.

Fix X,A,s,δ and assume L1: s>0 and δ>0. Set c=C^s_δ(A), possibly ∞. Take any sequence V and assume L2: V is a δ-cover of A×I in MaxProd(X). Put ρ_i=diam(V_i), A_i=π_X(V_i), B_i=π_ℝ(V_i). Every V_i is bounded, since its extended diameter is ≤δ<∞. Each projection has pairwise distances at most ρ_i, whence diam A_i≤ρ_i and diam B_i≤ρ_i≤δ. For a nonempty V_i, B_i is nonempty and bounded above and below: choose any one of its points and use the finite diameter bound. Thus inf B_i and sup B_i exist as real numbers. Put J_i=[inf B_i,sup B_i]. The least-upper-bound and greatest-lower-bound properties give B_i⊆J_i and sup B_i-inf B_i≤ρ_i: for every b,b'∈B_i one has b-b'≤ρ_i, and taking supremum in b then infimum in b' preserves the inequality. In particular inf B_i≤sup B_i. For empty V_i put ρ_i=0 and A_i=B_i=J_i=∅. Each J_i is a closed real interval or ∅, hence Borel measurable, and all projection bounds remain valid. This construction imposes no measurability on V_i or its projections.

For each nonempty member, apply M009 with endpoints inf B_i and sup B_i. By F001, volume(J_i)=ofReal(sup B_i-inf B_i)≤ρ_i. For an empty member volume(J_i)=volume(∅)=0=ρ_i by the empty-set axiom of a measure. Also I=[0,1] is closed and measurable and M009 with endpoints 0,1 gives volume(I)=1. Since I∩J_i⊆J_i, measure monotonicity gives volume(I∩J_i)≤volume(J_i)≤ρ_i; each intersection is measurable as an intersection of closed measurable sets.

Define g(t)=1_I(t)c and f_seq(i)(t)=1_{I∩J_i}(t)ρ_i^s. Fix any real t. In the case L3: t∈I, the family consisting of A_i when t∈J_i and ∅ otherwise covers A: under the auxiliary antecedent L4: x∈A, L2 supplies an i with (x,t)∈V_i, so x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. This proves membership in the projected union; discharge L4 and quantify x. Each such projected set has diameter ≤ρ_i≤δ by F001. N001 therefore gives c≤Σ_i ρ_i^s 1_{J_i}(t)=Σ_i f_seq(i)(t). Discharge L3 after the inside-I argument. If t∉I, g(t)=0 and every f_seq(i)(t)=0 by the indicator zero branch, so the same inequality holds. Universal introduction in t gives g≤Σ_i f_seq(i) pointwise on ℝ, also if c=∞. F002 shows that every indicator summand is Borel measurable: its only values are a nonnegative constant and zero on complementary measurable pieces, hence it is also volume-almost-everywhere measurable. No product of an undefined infinite real quantity is used.

Integrate F003 over ℝ with Lebesgue measure. M011 gives lintegral(volume,g)≤lintegral(volume,Σ_i f_seq(i)). M012 for I and constant c, together with volume(I)=1 from F002, gives lintegral(volume,g)=c·1=c, even when c=∞. M010 for the countable family f_seq exchanges the nonnegative series and lower integral, since F003 established almost-everywhere measurability of each summand. M012 for I∩J_i and constant ρ_i^s evaluates each term. Thus
c=c·volume(I)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s volume(I∩J_i)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s volume(J_i)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s ρ_i
 =Σ_i ρ_i^(s+1).
The middle bounds use F002 and monotonicity of multiplication and nonnegative sums. Each ρ_i is finite and nonnegative, and ρ_i^s·ρ_i=ρ_i^(s+1) holds for positive ρ_i by the real-power law and for ρ_i=0 because s>0. This is an ℝ≥0∞ computation; neither c nor the series need be finite. Discharge L2: every admissible δ-cover has (s+1)-cost at least c.

By the lower-infimum bound in N001, F004 implies C^s_δ(A)≤C^(s+1)_δ(A×I), including if no admissible product cover exists. This holds at every δ>0. Taking suprema over positive scales and using N001 for both positive exponents s and s+1 gives H^s(A)≤H^(s+1)(A×I). Discharge L1 and universally quantify X,A,s and the scale. These are the complete scale and measure inequalities asserted in the output proposition.

Define e_h=e_basis(h) by the standard coordinate formula: its h-th coordinate is 1 and every other coordinate is 0. The n₀ coordinate unit vectors form a real basis of Rn(n₀): every vector is its finite coordinate linear combination, and equality of coordinates forces all coefficients in a zero combination to vanish. There are n₀ vectors. For n₀=0 this is the empty basis of the zero vector space. In MaxProd(Rn(n₀)), the n₀ vectors (e_h,0) together with (0,1) similarly span uniquely, by the first coordinates and last coordinate, so its real dimension is n₀+1. Both are real normed vector spaces (the second with the maximum product norm) and finite dimensional. Apply M007 to their full spaces and M006 to E⊆univ Rn(n₀) and F⊆univ MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). We obtain 0≤D≤n₀ and 0≤T≤n₀+1. The lower zero bounds follow from the ℝ≥0∞ codomain of dimH. Thus D and T are finite, including when n₀=0. A finite extended nonnegative real is the cast of its unique nonnegative real representative, and casts preserve finite sums and order.

The real line has basis {1}, hence real dimension one. The set I=[0,1] contains the open interval (0,1) in its interior: for each of its points the distance to the two endpoints has a positive minimum, giving a contained open ball. In particular 1/2 belongs to the interior. Apply M013 to the real normed space ℝ and A=I. Its hypotheses hold and it gives dimH(I)=1.

H001 supplies x_f∈E. Define f_f(t)=(x_f,t). For any real t,u, the maximum product distance between f_f(t) and f_f(u) is max(dist(x_f,x_f),|t-u|)=|t-u|. Thus f_f is an isometry; its image of I is {x_f}×I, a subset of F by x_f∈E.

Apply M008 to f_f and I, using the isometry in F003. It gives dimH(f_f '' I)=dimH(I)=1 by F002. Apply M006 to f_f '' I⊆F, also in F003, to get 1≤dimH(F)=T. Combining with F001 proves 0≤D≤n₀<∞ and 1≤T≤n₀+1<∞, together with dimH(I)=1 and the finite real identifications. The chosen point and its map do not occur in the output proposition.
By N004, write D and T as casts of finite real values d_real≥0 and k_real≥1, respectively. Order and addition of these finite values agree with their real operations.

Fix arbitrary real q and assume L1: q>d_real. F001 gives q>0, so q defines a nonnegative real exponent. M003 with set E and exponent q gives H^q(E)=0, since dimH(E)=D<q. Apply N002 to X=Rn(n₀), A=E and q. Its positive-exponent and zero-measure premises have just been established, and E×I in MaxProd(Rn(n₀)) is F. Therefore H^(q+1)(F)=0.

Since q+1>0, it is also a nonnegative real exponent. By F002 its Hausdorff measure on F is zero, hence different from ∞. Apply M004 with F and exponent q+1. It gives T≤q+1, equivalently k_real≤q+1 by F001. Discharge L1: for every real q>d_real one has k_real≤q+1.

Assume for contradiction L2: k_real>d_real+1. Put q_mid=(d_real+k_real-1)/2. Then d_real<q_mid<k_real-1, because k_real-1>d_real. F003 with q=q_mid gives k_real≤q_mid+1<k_real, a contradiction. Discharge L2 to obtain k_real≤d_real+1. Cast back by F001: T≤D+1. Finiteness is already supplied by F001. This proves the output proposition for every natural n₀, including zero.

By N004 write D,T as casts of real values d_real≥0 and k_real≥1. Their orders and addition agree with real operations. If L3: d_real=0, the fibre bound k_real≥1 gives k_real≥d_real+1. Discharge L3 to retain this implication. Since d_real≥0, the other case is d_real>0.

Assume L1: d_real>0. To prove the lower bound, assume for contradiction L2: k_real<d_real+1. Then 0≤k_real-1<d_real by F001. Put s_mid=(k_real-1+d_real)/2. These inequalities imply 0<s_mid<d_real and k_real<s_mid+1. The strict positivity of s_mid follows from d_real>0 even if k_real-1=0.

By F002, M002 applied to E at the nonnegative exponent s_mid gives H^s_mid(E)=∞, because dimH(E)=D is the cast of d_real. N003, applied with X=Rn(n₀), A=E and s=s_mid, gives H^s_mid(E)≤H^(s_mid+1)(F). Consequently H^(s_mid+1)(F)=∞.

M005 with A=F and the nonnegative exponent s_mid+1 yields s_mid+1≤T from F003, equivalently s_mid+1≤k_real by F001. This contradicts F002. Discharge L2 and conclude k_real≥d_real+1 under L1. Discharge L1, and combine with the d_real=0 implication in F001 by exhaustive cases on d_real≥0. Hence k_real≥d_real+1 for all cases.

F004 gives T≥D+1, and N005 gives T≤D+1. Antisymmetry proves T=D+1. Both dimensions and their sum are finite by F001 and N004. When n₀=0, N004 forces D=0 and the fibre branch already supplies the lower bound; the upper proof also covered this case. This proves the output proposition. Compactness remains an original hypothesis in the global specification, although this replacement proof does not use it.

Fix arbitrary p,z∈L2Prod(n₀). Apply M014 with W=Rn(n₀), Z=ℝ and argument p-z. These are normed additive commutative groups, hence satisfy its seminormed assumptions. With the coordinatewise subtraction and distance as norm of difference, the source gives
 dist(p,z)²=‖p.fst-z.fst‖²+|p.snd-z.snd|²
 =Σ_{h<n₀}|p.fst_h-z.fst_h|²+|p.snd-z.snd|².
The second equality uses the defining squared Euclidean norm on Rn(n₀). On the other hand, the defining squared norm on Rn(n₀+1), split into its first n₀ coordinates and last coordinate, gives
 dist(j(n₀)(p),j(n₀)(z))²=Σ_{h<n₀}|p.fst_h-z.fst_h|²+|p.snd-z.snd|².
The two nonnegative distances have equal squares; hence they are equal. These formulas hold also when n₀=0, with an empty finite sum.

By F001, j(n₀) is an isometry. Its explicit inverse sends a vector v∈Rn(n₀+1) to the pair consisting of its first n₀ coordinates in Rn(n₀) and its last coordinate, regarded as an element of L2Prod(n₀) using euclideanLift n₀. Coordinate evaluation shows that both composites are the identity. Hence j(n₀) is bijective. By the definitions of F,G,euclideanLift and j, a point of j(n₀) '' (euclideanLift n₀ '' F) is precisely a concatenation of x∈E and t∈I; conversely every such concatenation arises this way. Thus this image equals G. For arbitrary x,y∈Rn(n₀) and real t,u, specialize F001 with p_bound=euclideanLift n₀ (x,t) and z_bound=euclideanLift n₀ (y,u) to obtain the squared-distance formula stated in the output proposition for every such x,y,t,u. For n₀=0 the inverse still extracts the last coordinate and the empty initial tuple; every step is unchanged.

Apply the exact prepared basis port E001 with its universally bound n equal to the current n₀ and S=F⊆MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). Its identity map on underlying pairs is euclideanLift n₀, with image in L2Prod(n₀). It gives dimH(euclideanLift n₀ '' F)=dimH(F)=T. This is exactly the registered maximum-to-L² product dimension equality.

N007 proves that j(n₀):L2Prod(n₀)→Rn(n₀+1) is an isometry and that j(n₀) '' (euclideanLift n₀ '' F)=G. Apply M008 with this map and set euclideanLift n₀ '' F. It gives dimH(G)=dimH(euclideanLift n₀ '' F). By F001 and N006 this equals T=D+1=dimH(E)+1. N006 also provides finiteness. By D016, G is exactly the specified Euclidean E×[0,1] under coordinate concatenation, and E on the right retains its original Euclidean Rn(n₀) metric. N007 includes the n₀=0 identification, so there is no excluded ambient dimension. Since the dimensions are finite, the extended nonnegative equality is also equality of the real Hausdorff dimensions. This is the complete selected conclusion.

import Mathlib
open scoped ENNReal NNReal Topology
open Set MeasureTheory
namespace BasisObjects
abbrev Rn (n : ℕ) := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)
noncomputable def content {X : Type*} [EMetricSpace X]
    (s : ℝ) (r : ℝ≥0∞) (A : Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨅ (U : ℕ → Set X) (_ : A ⊆ ⋃ i, U i)
    (_ : ∀ i, Metric.ediam (U i) ≤ r),
      ∑' i, ⨆ (_ : (U i).Nonempty), (Metric.ediam (U i)) ^ s
def euclideanLift (n : ℕ) : Rn n × ℝ → WithLp 2 (Rn n × ℝ) :=
  WithLp.toLp 2
end BasisObjects

namespace IntervalProduct
abbrev Rn := BasisObjects.Rn
def I : Set ℝ := Set.Icc 0 1
def F (n : ℕ) (E : Set (Rn n)) : Set (Rn n × ℝ) := E ×ˢ I
def j (n : ℕ) (p : WithLp 2 (Rn n × ℝ)) : Rn (n + 1) :=
  WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.snoc (fun i => p.fst i) p.snd)
def unj (n : ℕ) (v : Rn (n + 1)) : WithLp 2 (Rn n × ℝ) :=
  WithLp.toLp 2 (WithLp.toLp 2 (fun i : Fin n => v i.castSucc), v (Fin.last n))
def G (n : ℕ) (E : Set (Rn n)) : Set (Rn (n + 1)) :=
  j n '' (BasisObjects.euclideanLift n '' F n E)
noncomputable def H {X : Type*} [MetricSpace X] (a : ℝ) (A : Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  letI : MeasurableSpace X := borel X
  letI : BorelSpace X := ⟨rfl⟩
  MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure a A
noncomputable def cost {ι X : Type*} [MetricSpace X] (a : ℝ) (U : ι → Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ∑' i, ⨆ (_ : (U i).Nonempty), (Metric.ediam (U i)) ^ a
noncomputable def realCost {ι X : Type*} [MetricSpace X] (a : ℝ) (U : ι → Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ∑' i, (ENNReal.ofReal (Metric.diam (U i))) ^ a
def Cover {X : Type*} [MetricSpace X] (δ : ℝ) (A : Set X) (U : ℕ → Set X) : Prop :=
  A ⊆ ⋃ i, U i ∧ ∀ i, Metric.ediam (U i) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal δ
def RealCover {X : Type*} [MetricSpace X] (δ : ℝ) (A : Set X) (U : ℕ → Set X) : Prop :=
  A ⊆ ⋃ i, U i ∧ (∀ i, Bornology.IsBounded (U i)) ∧ ∀ i, Metric.diam (U i) ≤ δ
end IntervalProduct
open IntervalProduct

∀ (X : Type*) [MetricSpace X] (A : Set X) (a : ℝ), 0 < a →
  (∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ →
    BasisObjects.content a (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A =
      ⨅ (U : ℕ → Set X) (_ : RealCover δ A U), realCost a U) ∧
  (∀ (ι : Type*) [Countable ι] (V : ι → Set X),
    ∃ e : ι ↪ ℕ, ∃ U : ℕ → Set X,
      (∀ k, U (e k) = V k) ∧
      (∀ i, i ∉ Set.range e → U i = ∅) ∧
      (⋃ i, U i) = (⋃ k, V k) ∧
      cost a U = cost a V ∧ realCost a U = realCost a V) ∧
  (∀ δ₁ δ₂ : ℝ, 0 < δ₁ → δ₁ ≤ δ₂ →
    BasisObjects.content a (ENNReal.ofReal δ₂) A ≤
      BasisObjects.content a (ENNReal.ofReal δ₁) A) ∧
  (∀ (δ : ℝ) (U : ℕ → Set X), 0 < δ → Cover δ A U →
    BasisObjects.content a (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A ≤ cost a U) ∧
  (∀ (δ : ℝ) (b : ℝ≥0∞), 0 < δ →
    (∀ U : ℕ → Set X, Cover δ A U → b ≤ cost a U) →
      b ≤ BasisObjects.content a (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A) ∧
  (H a A = ⨆ (δ : ℝ) (_ : 0 < δ), BasisObjects.content a (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A) ∧
  (∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → BasisObjects.content a (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A ≤ H a A) ∧
  (∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ →
    (BasisObjects.content a (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A = 0 ↔
      ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ U : ℕ → Set X, Cover δ A U ∧ cost a U < ENNReal.ofReal ε)) ∧
  (H a A = 0 ↔
    ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε →
      ∃ U : ℕ → Set X, Cover δ A U ∧ cost a U < ENNReal.ofReal ε)
steps.explanation: Complete N001 package: identify the guarded extended-diameter infima with bounded real-diameter covers at positive scale; explicitly reindex arbitrary countable families with empty padding and equal union/cost; prove scale monotonicity, both infimum bounds, positive-real-scale supremum, and the two zero/cheap-cover equivalences. Use the pinned hausdorffMeasure_apply formula directly with the Borel structure fixed by H. No measurability or boundedness of A is assumed; the empty admissible family has infimum ∞. Strict inequalities compare with ofReal ε only when ε>0.

steps.statement:
∀ (X : Type*) [MetricSpace X] (A : Set X) (q : ℝ), 0 < q → H q A = 0 →
  ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε →
    ∃ U : ℕ → Set (X × ℝ), Cover δ (A ×ˢ I) U ∧ cost (q + 1) U < ENNReal.ofReal ε
steps.explanation: Existing upper covering construction only. At r=min(1,δ), take the q-cost <ε/4 cover from N001; add positive numerical radii with geometric q-cost ≤ε/4, without changing sets. The radii are at most r and one. Subdivide I into ceil(1/r_i) closed intervals, use the maximum metric and N_i≤2/r_i, then reindex the countable family of finite products. The obligation retains all positive scale/tolerance quantifiers and allows empty and zero-diameter members.

steps.statement:
∀ (X : Type*) [MetricSpace X] (A : Set X) (q : ℝ), 0 < q → H q A = 0 →

steps.statement:

    BasisObjects.content s (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A ≤ cost (s + 1) V
steps.explanation: For an arbitrary product cover, derive boundedness from its finite diameter bound, project the sets, and enclose each nonempty real projection by its closed [inf,sup] hull (empty members use ∅). Hulls are Borel, contain the projections, and have volume at most the member diameter. The selected projected sets cover each fibre t∈I. Integrate the resulting indicator inequality over ℝ. The series interchange uses a.e. measurability of each nonnegative indicator summand; no finiteness or integrability is required. Keep c and every series in ℝ≥0∞, including c=∞. Apply the direct library interval measure, lintegral monotonicity, lintegral_tsum and indicator-constant formulas with their actual conditions. For the zero-diameter power identity use s>0.

steps.statement:
∀ (X : Type*) [MetricSpace X] (A : Set X) (s : ℝ), 0 < s →
  (∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ →
    BasisObjects.content s (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A ≤
      BasisObjects.content (s + 1) (ENNReal.ofReal δ) (A ×ˢ I)) ∧
  H s A ≤ H (s + 1) (A ×ˢ I)
steps.explanation: Export full N003 by the lower-infimum bound of N001 applied to T004, even when there is no admissible cover. Take suprema over positive real scales at exponents s and s+1 to obtain the Hausdorff-measure inequality. Both inequalities are unconditional in finiteness and require no measurability of A or covering sets.

steps.statement:
0 ≤ dimH E ∧ dimH E ≤ (n : ℝ≥0∞) ∧ (n : ℝ≥0∞) < ⊤ ∧

steps.explanation: Export N004 using coordinate bases to get finrank n and n+1 (including the empty basis at n=0), direct Mathlib full-space dimension and monotonicity, and the interval interior dimension formula. A point of E supplied by H001 gives the isometric fibre t↦(x,t), hence T≥1. The finite ENNReal bounds yield the stated NNReal representatives; casts preserve order and addition of finite values by the ordinary library identities. The chosen point does not escape. The quantified representatives are NNReal values d,k; their real coercions give d_real,k_real, and their ENNReal coercions recover D,T without any truncation.

steps.statement: dimH (F n E) ≤ dimH E + 1 ∧ dimH E < ⊤ ∧ dimH (F n E) < ⊤
steps.explanation: Export N005. Choose the finite representatives from N004. For every real q>d, q>0; apply the critical-exponent zero-measure theorem to E at the NNReal exponent determined by q, N002, and the dimension upper bound from measure ≠∞. A contrary strict upper inequality is refuted at the source midpoint q=(d+k-1)/2. Cast the resulting finite-real inequality back to ENNReal. The direct library critical-exponent declarations quantify NNReal exponents, so positivity supplies the needed nonnegative subtype and its real coercion.

steps.explanation: Export N006 on the original domain. For the finite real representatives d,k, handle d=0 using the fibre bound k≥1. If d>0 and k<d+1, use the source midpoint s=(k-1+d)/2; it is positive, less than d, and s+1>k. The critical-exponent infinite-measure theorem, N003 and the dimension lower bound from infinite measure contradict this. Antisymmetry with N005 gives equality. N004 gives finiteness and includes n=0. H002 remains an original project premise although this source argument does not use compactness.

steps.statement:
Isometry (j n) ∧ Function.Bijective (j n) ∧
  Function.LeftInverse (unj n) (j n) ∧ Function.RightInverse (unj n) (j n) ∧
  j n '' (BasisObjects.euclideanLift n '' F n E) = G n E ∧
  ∀ (x y : Rn n) (t u : ℝ),
    (dist (j n (BasisObjects.euclideanLift n (x,t)))
      (j n (BasisObjects.euclideanLift n (y,u)))) ^ 2 =

    (dist (BasisObjects.euclideanLift n (x,t))
      (BasisObjects.euclideanLift n (y,u))) ^ 2 =
      (∑ h : Fin n, |x h - y h| ^ 2) + |t - u| ^ 2
steps.explanation: Export full N007 in the fixed Euclidean representations. Split squared L² product norm into its two coordinate norms and expand the Euclidean norm as the finite coordinate sum; split the concatenated sum at Fin.last. Equal squares of nonnegative distances give Isometry j. Check both composites with the explicit truncation/last-coordinate unj, and identify the image set. The last conjunct records the squared-distance identity for all x,y,t,u. n=0 is retained with an empty initial sum. The metric bridge is a proved obligation, not a definition of an isometry.

steps.explanation: Instantiate the exact E001 port at n and S=F n E to transport dimH from the maximum product to its L² image. Apply isometry invariance to j from N007 and its explicit image G, then use N006. This gives the complete target equality and transfers finiteness to G. H001 and H002 remain the exact original nonempty/compact assumptions in the exported project theorem; no positivity assumption on n is introduced.
