value.text: Fix X,A,a and assume L1: a>0. Work with X's Borel structure, so M001 applies and gives H^a(A)=sup_{r>0} content(a,r,A) over extended nonnegative r. For arbitrary δ, temporarily assume L2: δ>0. At the finite scale ofReal δ, every admissible covering member has finite extended diameter, hence is bounded and has ediam equal to its real diameter cast to ℝ≥0∞. The nonemptiness-proof supremum in D004 is the displayed diameter power on a nonempty member and is zero on an empty member. For a>0 this agrees with assigning the empty member diameter zero and 0^a=0. Thus the nested infima are exactly the original admissible-cover infimum, with no prefactor. A finite family can be padded by empty sets. For an arbitrary countable index type choose an injection into ℕ; at each image index put the unique original member and elsewhere put ∅. This preserves the union and all nonnegative sums. Conversely an ℕ-family is countable. Discharge L2 after this finite-scale interpretation, retaining its δ>0 antecedent for every δ. For arbitrary δ₁,δ₂, temporarily assume L3: 0<δ₁≤δ₂. Every δ₁-cover is a δ₂-cover, so C^a_δ₂(A)≤C^a_δ₁(A). Discharge L3 and quantify the two scales. Every cost bounds its infimum above; a lower bound on every admissible cost bounds the infimum below. If the admissible family is empty its infimum is ∞, and the latter assertion remains true. For any positive extended scale r, if it is finite it is the cast of a positive real scale. The content at r=∞ is at most that at any fixed finite positive scale, since every finite-scale cover is also an ∞-cover. Hence the ∞ scale adds nothing to the supremum. We have proved H^a(A)=sup_{δ>0}C^a_δ(A), and each such content is ≤H^a(A).

For the arbitrary δ,ε, temporarily assume L4: δ>0 and ε>0. Suppose L5: C^a_δ(A)=0. if every admissible cost were ≥ε, the lower-bound property in F001 would imply C^a_δ(A)≥ε>0, a contradiction. Thus an admissible cover of cost <ε exists. Discharge L5 to obtain the forward implication. In terms of the nested infima in D004, any failed cover or diameter condition has value ∞ and cannot give a value <ε, so the approximation provides an actual admissible family. Conversely assume L6: for every positive tolerance there exists an admissible cover of smaller cost. This forces the nonnegative content to be zero: a positive value, finite or infinite, has some positive finite real below it, contradicting the upper bound by those costs. Discharge L6, then L4, and quantify the arbitrary positive scale and tolerance. This proves the zero-content approximation equivalence for every positive scale. These arguments also cover an empty admissible family, whose content is ∞.

By F001, H^a(A)=0 implies each positive-scale content is zero; F002 then gives the required arbitrarily small covers at every scale. Conversely, those covers make every positive-scale content zero by F002, and their supremum is zero by F001. This proves the full equivalence and all asserted content properties. Discharge L1 to retain a>0 as an antecedent and universally quantify X,A,a and the scale/tolerance variables. No boundedness or measurability assumption on A is used.

Fix X,A,q and assume L1: q>0 and H^q(A)=0. Fix arbitrary real δ,ε and assume L2: δ>0 and ε>0. Put r=min(1,δ), so 0<r≤1 and r≤δ. By N001 with exponent q, scale r and tolerance ε/4 there exists a countable r-cover U of A whose total q-cost is <ε/4; reindex it as a sequence with empty padding if necessary. In particular its members have finite diameter.

Choose U from F001 and put d_i=diam(U_i), with d_i=0 on empty members. For each natural i define a_seq(i)=min(r,(ε·2^(-i-3))^(1/q)). Both entries of this minimum are positive, so 0<a_seq(i)≤r and a_seq(i)^q≤ε·2^(-i-3). The nonnegative geometric series has sum Σ_{i≥0}2^(-i-3)=1/4 (its partial sums are (1/4)(1-2^(-m)) for the first m terms). Hence Σ a_seq(i)^q≤ε/4. Put r_i=max(d_i,a_seq(i)). Then 0<r_i≤r≤1 and r_i^q=max(d_i^q,a_seq(i)^q)≤d_i^q+a_seq(i)^q. Summing nonnegative terms, using F001 and the geometric bound, gives Σ r_i^q<ε/2. Numerical padding changes no covering set and works even if X is a singleton.

For each natural i put N_i=ceil(1/r_i), a positive integer. Then 1/N_i≤r_i and N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i, since 0<r_i≤1. The closed intervals [h/N_i,(h+1)/N_i], 0≤h<N_i, cover I. Define W_seq(i,h)=U_i×[h/N_i,(h+1)/N_i]. In the maximum product metric any two points of this product have distance at most r_i, since the first-coordinate diameter is d_i≤r_i and the second-coordinate interval length is 1/N_i≤r_i. The product family covers A×I, and its index set {(i,h):i∈ℕ,0≤h<N_i} is countable. Empty products have zero cost. By N001 this countable family may be reindexed into ℕ without changing the union or sum. It is a δ-cover, and its total (q+1)-cost is at most Σ_i N_i r_i^(q+1)≤2Σ_i r_i^q<ε. The power cancellation r_i^(q+1)/r_i=r_i^q is valid because r_i>0. Rearranging these nonnegative sums is legitimate, and the upper bound is finite.

F003 holds for arbitrary positive δ,ε. Discharge L2 to obtain existence of the stated arbitrarily fine arbitrarily cheap covers. Since q+1>0, N001, now for MaxProd(X), A×I and exponent q+1, implies H^(q+1)(A×I)=0. Discharge L1 and universally quantify X,A,q. This proves the output proposition on the whole asserted domain without any positive-diameter assumption on the covering sets.

Fix X,A,s,δ and assume L1: s>0 and δ>0. Set c=C^s_δ(A), possibly ∞. Take any sequence V and assume L2: V is a δ-cover of A×I in MaxProd(X). Put ρ_i=diam(V_i), A_i=π_X(V_i), B_i=π_ℝ(V_i). Every V_i is bounded, since its extended diameter is ≤δ<∞. Each projection has pairwise distances at most ρ_i, whence diam A_i≤ρ_i and diam B_i≤ρ_i≤δ. For a nonempty V_i, B_i is nonempty and bounded above and below: choose any one of its points and use the finite diameter bound. Thus inf B_i and sup B_i exist as real numbers. Put J_i=[inf B_i,sup B_i]. The least-upper-bound and greatest-lower-bound properties give B_i⊆J_i and sup B_i-inf B_i≤ρ_i: for every b,b'∈B_i one has b-b'≤ρ_i, and taking supremum in b then infimum in b' preserves the inequality. In particular inf B_i≤sup B_i. For empty V_i put ρ_i=0 and A_i=B_i=J_i=∅. Each J_i is a closed real interval or ∅, hence Borel measurable, and all projection bounds remain valid. This construction imposes no measurability on V_i or its projections.

For each nonempty member, apply M009 with endpoints inf B_i and sup B_i. By F001, volume(J_i)=ofReal(sup B_i-inf B_i)≤ρ_i. For an empty member volume(J_i)=volume(∅)=0=ρ_i by the empty-set axiom of a measure. Also I=[0,1] is closed and measurable and M009 with endpoints 0,1 gives volume(I)=1. Since I∩J_i⊆J_i, measure monotonicity gives volume(I∩J_i)≤volume(J_i)≤ρ_i; each intersection is measurable as an intersection of closed measurable sets.

Define g(t)=1_I(t)c and f_seq(i)(t)=1_{I∩J_i}(t)ρ_i^s. Fix any real t. In the case L3: t∈I, the family consisting of A_i when t∈J_i and ∅ otherwise covers A: under the auxiliary antecedent L4: x∈A, L2 supplies an i with (x,t)∈V_i, so x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. This proves membership in the projected union; discharge L4 and quantify x. Each such projected set has diameter ≤ρ_i≤δ by F001. N001 therefore gives c≤Σ_i ρ_i^s 1_{J_i}(t)=Σ_i f_seq(i)(t). Discharge L3 after the inside-I argument. If t∉I, g(t)=0 and every f_seq(i)(t)=0 by the indicator zero branch, so the same inequality holds. Universal introduction in t gives g≤Σ_i f_seq(i) pointwise on ℝ, also if c=∞. F002 shows that every indicator summand is Borel measurable: its only values are a nonnegative constant and zero on complementary measurable pieces, hence it is also volume-almost-everywhere measurable. No product of an undefined infinite real quantity is used.

Integrate F003 over ℝ with Lebesgue measure. M011 gives lintegral(volume,g)≤lintegral(volume,Σ_i f_seq(i)). M012 for I and constant c, together with volume(I)=1 from F002, gives lintegral(volume,g)=c·1=c, even when c=∞. M010 for the countable family f_seq exchanges the nonnegative series and lower integral, since F003 established almost-everywhere measurability of each summand. M012 for I∩J_i and constant ρ_i^s evaluates each term. Thus
c=c·volume(I)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s volume(I∩J_i)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s volume(J_i)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s ρ_i
 =Σ_i ρ_i^(s+1).
The middle bounds use F002 and monotonicity of multiplication and nonnegative sums. Each ρ_i is finite and nonnegative, and ρ_i^s·ρ_i=ρ_i^(s+1) holds for positive ρ_i by the real-power law and for ρ_i=0 because s>0. This is an ℝ≥0∞ computation; neither c nor the series need be finite. Discharge L2: every admissible δ-cover has (s+1)-cost at least c.

By the lower-infimum bound in N001, F004 implies C^s_δ(A)≤C^(s+1)_δ(A×I), including if no admissible product cover exists. This holds at every δ>0. Taking suprema over positive scales and using N001 for both positive exponents s and s+1 gives H^s(A)≤H^(s+1)(A×I). Discharge L1 and universally quantify X,A,s and the scale. These are the complete scale and measure inequalities asserted in the output proposition.

Define e_h=e_basis(h) by the standard coordinate formula: its h-th coordinate is 1 and every other coordinate is 0. The n₀ coordinate unit vectors form a real basis of Rn(n₀): every vector is its finite coordinate linear combination, and equality of coordinates forces all coefficients in a zero combination to vanish. There are n₀ vectors. For n₀=0 this is the empty basis of the zero vector space. In MaxProd(Rn(n₀)), the n₀ vectors (e_h,0) together with (0,1) similarly span uniquely, by the first coordinates and last coordinate, so its real dimension is n₀+1. Both are real normed vector spaces (the second with the maximum product norm) and finite dimensional. Apply M007 to their full spaces and M006 to E⊆univ Rn(n₀) and F⊆univ MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). We obtain 0≤D≤n₀ and 0≤T≤n₀+1. The lower zero bounds follow from the ℝ≥0∞ codomain of dimH. Thus D and T are finite, including when n₀=0. A finite extended nonnegative real is the cast of its unique nonnegative real representative, and casts preserve finite sums and order.

The real line has basis {1}, hence real dimension one. The set I=[0,1] contains the open interval (0,1) in its interior: for each of its points the distance to the two endpoints has a positive minimum, giving a contained open ball. In particular 1/2 belongs to the interior. Apply M013 to the real normed space ℝ and A=I. Its hypotheses hold and it gives dimH(I)=1.

H001 supplies x_f∈E. Define f_f(t)=(x_f,t). For any real t,u, the maximum product distance between f_f(t) and f_f(u) is max(dist(x_f,x_f),|t-u|)=|t-u|. Thus f_f is an isometry; its image of I is {x_f}×I, a subset of F by x_f∈E.

Apply M008 to f_f and I, using the isometry in F003. It gives dimH(f_f '' I)=dimH(I)=1 by F002. Apply M006 to f_f '' I⊆F, also in F003, to get 1≤dimH(F)=T. Combining with F001 proves 0≤D≤n₀<∞ and 1≤T≤n₀+1<∞, together with dimH(I)=1 and the finite real identifications. The chosen point and its map do not occur in the output proposition.
By N004, write D and T as casts of finite real values d_real≥0 and k_real≥1, respectively. Order and addition of these finite values agree with their real operations.

Fix arbitrary real q and assume L1: q>d_real. F001 gives q>0, so q defines a nonnegative real exponent. M003 with set E and exponent q gives H^q(E)=0, since dimH(E)=D<q. Apply N002 to X=Rn(n₀), A=E and q. Its positive-exponent and zero-measure premises have just been established, and E×I in MaxProd(Rn(n₀)) is F. Therefore H^(q+1)(F)=0.

Since q+1>0, it is also a nonnegative real exponent. By F002 its Hausdorff measure on F is zero, hence different from ∞. Apply M004 with F and exponent q+1. It gives T≤q+1, equivalently k_real≤q+1 by F001. Discharge L1: for every real q>d_real one has k_real≤q+1.

Assume for contradiction L2: k_real>d_real+1. Put q_mid=(d_real+k_real-1)/2. Then d_real<q_mid<k_real-1, because k_real-1>d_real. F003 with q=q_mid gives k_real≤q_mid+1<k_real, a contradiction. Discharge L2 to obtain k_real≤d_real+1. Cast back by F001: T≤D+1. Finiteness is already supplied by F001. This proves the output proposition for every natural n₀, including zero.

By N004 write D,T as casts of real values d_real≥0 and k_real≥1. Their orders and addition agree with real operations. If L3: d_real=0, the fibre bound k_real≥1 gives k_real≥d_real+1. Discharge L3 to retain this implication. Since d_real≥0, the other case is d_real>0.

Assume L1: d_real>0. To prove the lower bound, assume for contradiction L2: k_real<d_real+1. Then 0≤k_real-1<d_real by F001. Put s_mid=(k_real-1+d_real)/2. These inequalities imply 0<s_mid<d_real and k_real<s_mid+1. The strict positivity of s_mid follows from d_real>0 even if k_real-1=0.

By F002, M002 applied to E at the nonnegative exponent s_mid gives H^s_mid(E)=∞, because dimH(E)=D is the cast of d_real. N003, applied with X=Rn(n₀), A=E and s=s_mid, gives H^s_mid(E)≤H^(s_mid+1)(F). Consequently H^(s_mid+1)(F)=∞.

M005 with A=F and the nonnegative exponent s_mid+1 yields s_mid+1≤T from F003, equivalently s_mid+1≤k_real by F001. This contradicts F002. Discharge L2 and conclude k_real≥d_real+1 under L1. Discharge L1, and combine with the d_real=0 implication in F001 by exhaustive cases on d_real≥0. Hence k_real≥d_real+1 for all cases.

F004 gives T≥D+1, and N005 gives T≤D+1. Antisymmetry proves T=D+1. Both dimensions and their sum are finite by F001 and N004. When n₀=0, N004 forces D=0 and the fibre branch already supplies the lower bound; the upper proof also covered this case. This proves the output proposition. Compactness remains an original hypothesis in the global specification, although this replacement proof does not use it.

Fix arbitrary p,z∈L2Prod(n₀). Apply M014 with W=Rn(n₀), Z=ℝ and argument p-z. These are normed additive commutative groups, hence satisfy its seminormed assumptions. With the coordinatewise subtraction and distance as norm of difference, the source gives
 dist(p,z)²=‖p.fst-z.fst‖²+|p.snd-z.snd|²
 =Σ_{h<n₀}|p.fst_h-z.fst_h|²+|p.snd-z.snd|².
The second equality uses the defining squared Euclidean norm on Rn(n₀). On the other hand, the defining squared norm on Rn(n₀+1), split into its first n₀ coordinates and last coordinate, gives
 dist(j(n₀)(p),j(n₀)(z))²=Σ_{h<n₀}|p.fst_h-z.fst_h|²+|p.snd-z.snd|².
The two nonnegative distances have equal squares; hence they are equal. These formulas hold also when n₀=0, with an empty finite sum.

By F001, j(n₀) is an isometry. Its explicit inverse sends a vector v∈Rn(n₀+1) to the pair consisting of its first n₀ coordinates in Rn(n₀) and its last coordinate, regarded as an element of L2Prod(n₀) using euclideanLift n₀. Coordinate evaluation shows that both composites are the identity. Hence j(n₀) is bijective. By the definitions of F,G,euclideanLift and j, a point of j(n₀) '' (euclideanLift n₀ '' F) is precisely a concatenation of x∈E and t∈I; conversely every such concatenation arises this way. Thus this image equals G. For arbitrary x,y∈Rn(n₀) and real t,u, specialize F001 with p_bound=euclideanLift n₀ (x,t) and z_bound=euclideanLift n₀ (y,u) to obtain the squared-distance formula stated in the output proposition for every such x,y,t,u. For n₀=0 the inverse still extracts the last coordinate and the empty initial tuple; every step is unchanged.

Apply the exact prepared basis port E001 with its universally bound n equal to the current n₀ and S=F⊆MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). Its identity map on underlying pairs is euclideanLift n₀, with image in L2Prod(n₀). It gives dimH(euclideanLift n₀ '' F)=dimH(F)=T. This is exactly the registered maximum-to-L² product dimension equality.

N007 proves that j(n₀):L2Prod(n₀)→Rn(n₀+1) is an isometry and that j(n₀) '' (euclideanLift n₀ '' F)=G. Apply M008 with this map and set euclideanLift n₀ '' F. value.N001: For every metric space X, subset A⊆X and real a>0, the positive-scale contents C^a_δ(A) are exactly the unnormalized real-diameter countable-cover contents of the original problem. Finite or countable index families can be reindexed into ℕ with empty padding and unchanged cost. For 0<δ₁≤δ₂, C^a_δ₂(A)≤C^a_δ₁(A). Each admissible δ-cover has cost at least C^a_δ(A), and every lower bound for all admissible costs bounds C^a_δ(A) below (including when no cover exists). H^a(A)=sup_{δ>0} C^a_δ(A), so C^a_δ(A)≤H^a(A). For δ>0, C^a_δ(A)=0 iff for every real ε>0 there is an admissible countable δ-cover with a-cost <ε. Consequently H^a(A)=0 iff such covers exist at every positive δ and every positive ε. All costs and infima are in ℝ≥0∞; empty members contribute zero.
value.N002: For every metric space X, A⊆X and real q>0, H^q(A)=0 implies H^(q+1)(A×I)=0, with A×I regarded as a subset of MaxProd(X). Under the same premises q>0 and H^q(A)=0, for every δ>0 and ε>0 there is a countable δ-cover of A×I with (q+1)-cost <ε. This includes singleton and zero-dimensional metric spaces.
value.N003: For every metric space X, A⊆X, real s>0 and δ>0, C^s_δ(A)≤C^(s+1)_δ(A×I) in the maximum product metric MaxProd(X). Consequently H^s(A)≤H^(s+1)(A×I). These inequalities are in ℝ≥0∞; neither finiteness, compactness nor measurability of A or of the covering sets is required.
value.N004: 0≤D≤n₀<∞ and 1≤T≤n₀+1<∞, where D=dimH(E) in Euclidean Rn(n₀) and T=dimH(F) in MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). Also dimH(I)=1. In particular D and T have finite nonnegative real representatives, and their orders and addition by finite numbers agree with the corresponding ℝ≥0∞ operations. These assertions include n₀=0.
value.N005: T≤D+1 in ℝ≥0∞, for D=dimH(E) in Euclidean Rn(n₀) and T=dimH(F) in the maximum product metric. Both dimensions are finite, and this is equivalently the inequality between their nonnegative real representatives.
value.N006: T=D+1, where D=dimH(E) in Euclidean Rn(n₀) and T=dimH(F) in MaxProd(Rn(n₀)). Both sides are finite extended nonnegative reals. Equivalently, dimH(E×I)=dimH(E)+1 in the maximum product metric, for the original nonempty compact E and every natural n₀, including n₀=0.
value.N007: The coordinate concatenation map j(n₀):L2Prod(n₀)→Rn(n₀+1) is a bijective isometry for the library L² product norm and the Euclidean norm on Rn(n₀+1). Its inverse truncates the first n₀ coordinates and extracts the last coordinate. It sends euclideanLift n₀ '' F exactly to G. For any x,y∈Rn(n₀) and t,u∈ℝ, the squared distance of the concatenated points is Σ_{h<n₀}|x_h-y_h|²+|t-u|², equal to the squared L² product distance between euclideanLift n₀ (x,t) and euclideanLift n₀ (y,u). For n₀=0 the sum is empty and this is the usual identification of ℝ^0×ℝ with ℝ.
value.P: dimH(G)=dimH(E)+1, where E has its original Euclidean metric and G is E×[0,1] identified with Euclidean Rn(n₀+1) as specified in the selected target; this holds for every natural n₀, including n₀=0. Both sides are finite, so the equality also holds for real Hausdorff dimensions.

result.value:
Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
\(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.

Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.

Basis proof for the complete selected target. All Hausdorff measures below are unnormalized diameter measures: no dimensional prefactor, ball-radius convention, probability normalization, or new hypothesis is introduced. The only H is the original one: n is an arbitrary natural number and E⊆Euclidean ℝ^n is nonempty and compact. Write X=Rn(n), I=[0,1], F=E×I, and D=dim_H E. We use the maximum metric on X×ℝ during the covering argument and return to the required Euclidean metric in paragraph 8. The original proof route is replaced only as recorded in the replacements array. The B statements are dependencies with proofs/reductions, not a permission list restricting the freely available pinned Mathlib.

1. Content and normalization (B101 from B001). For a>0 and δ>0 let C^a_δ(A) be the infimum of Σ_i(diam U_i)^a over countable δ-covers of A. In Lean this is BasisObjects.content a (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A. A set with extended diameter ≤δ<∞ is bounded, and its extended diameter is the cast of its real diameter. Empty sets contribute zero: the header explicitly uses the supremum over a nonemptiness proof, which is zero when empty and is the unique displayed value when nonempty. This also agrees with 0^a=0 for a>0. A finite cover may be padded by empty sets. A cover with any countable index type can be enumerated with empty padding after an injection into ℕ, and conversely an ℕ-family is countable. The sums are unchanged. Thus these contents coincide exactly with those in the original problem. No normalizing constant occurs.

The admissible covers for δ₁≤δ₂ form nested families, giving C^a_δ₂≤C^a_δ₁. Each admissible cover bounds the infimum above. A bound from below for every admissible cover bounds its infimum below, also when there are no admissible covers (infimum of the empty family is ∞). B001 identifies H^a with the supremum of these contents over positive extended scales. Scales ∞ add nothing: content at ∞ is at most the content at any fixed finite positive scale. Every finite positive extended scale is the cast of a positive real scale. Hence H^a(A)=sup_{δ>0} C^a_δ(A), exactly the problem's convention. In particular every finite-scale content is ≤H^a.

2. Approximation of a zero content (completion of B101). In the complete lattice ℝ≥0∞, if the infimum of a family is zero then for every finite ε>0 some family member is <ε; otherwise ε is a positive lower bound. Apply this to the nested infima over U and the cover and diameter conditions. An unsuccessful condition has empty infimum and value ∞, so a value <ε provides an actual admissible U. Conversely covers of arbitrarily small positive cost make the content zero. Taking the supremum over δ proves: H^a(A)=0 iff at every positive scale there are countable covers of arbitrarily small positive a-cost. All costs and sums are interpreted in ℝ≥0∞; finite estimates can equivalently be written in nonnegative reals.

3. Upper cover construction (B102). Let X be any metric space, A⊆X, q>0 and H^q(A)=0. Fix a target scale δ>0 and ε>0. Put r=min(1,δ)>0. By paragraph 2 choose a countable r-cover U_i with Σ d_i^q<ε/4, where d_i=diam U_i (zero for empty sets). Choose numbers 0<a_i≤r with a_i^q≤ε 2^(-i-3). For example take the minimum of r and (ε 2^(-i-3))^(1/q); all quantities are positive. Then Σ a_i^q≤ε/4, since Σ_{i≥0}2^(-i-3)=1/4. Put r_i=max(d_i,a_i). These numbers satisfy 0<r_i≤r≤1, and r_i^q=max(d_i^q,a_i^q)≤d_i^q+a_i^q. Summing gives Σ r_i^q<ε/2. This numerical padding handles zero-diameter singletons in every metric space, including X=ℝ^0; no replacement ball or additional ambient point is required.

Let N_i=ceil(1/r_i), a positive integer. The intervals [j/N_i,(j+1)/N_i], 0≤j<N_i, cover I and have length 1/N_i≤r_i. Also N_i≤1/r_i+1≤2/r_i. The products U_i×[j/N_i,(j+1)/N_i] cover A×I. Their diameters in the maximum metric are at most r_i, because both coordinate distances are at most r_i. Empty products have cost zero. The index set {(i,j):i∈ℕ, j<N_i} is countable, so this is an admissible countable cover at scale δ. Its total (q+1)-cost is at most Σ_i N_i r_i^(q+1)≤2 Σ_i r_i^q<ε. The equality r_i^(q+1)/r_i=r_i^q is legitimate since every r_i>0. As δ and ε were arbitrary, paragraph 2 gives H^(q+1)(A×I)=0.

4. Lower slicing construction (B103). Let X be any metric space, A⊆X, s>0 and δ>0. Set c=C^s_δ(A), with c allowed to be ∞. Take any countable δ-cover V_i of A×I in the maximum product metric. For a nonempty V_i let ρ_i=diam V_i, A_i=π_X(V_i), and B_i=π_ℝ(V_i). Coordinate distances do not exceed product distances, so diam A_i≤ρ_i≤δ and diam B_i≤ρ_i. A nonempty B_i is bounded above and below, because it has finite diameter; define J_i=[inf B_i,sup B_i]. The defining least-upper-bound and greatest-lower-bound inequalities show B_i⊆J_i. They also show sup B_i-inf B_i≤ρ_i: every b-b' with b,b'∈B_i is ≤ρ_i, then take the supremum in b and infimum in b'. Consequently J_i is a measurable closed interval and B007 gives volume J_i≤ρ_i. For empty V_i put ρ_i=0, A_i=B_i=J_i=∅; all these conclusions still hold. Notice that this does not assert measurability of V_i, A_i or B_i.

For any t∈I, the family consisting of A_i when t∈J_i and ∅ otherwise is a δ-cover of A. Indeed (x,t) lies in some V_i whenever x∈A, and then x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. Therefore
c≤Σ_i ρ_i^s 1_{J_i}(t) for every t∈I.
Equivalently, on all of ℝ,
1_I(t)c ≤ Σ_i 1_{I∩J_i}(t)ρ_i^s.
Outside I both sides are zero; this also works for c=∞ because indicator functions use a zero branch, avoiding any ambiguous real multiplication. Every I∩J_i is measurable. Integrate this inequality with Lebesgue measure. B009 gives monotonicity, B010 evaluates the indicators, B007 gives volume I=1, and B008 exchanges the nonnegative series and lower integral. The result is
c=c·volume I
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s volume(I∩J_i)
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s volume J_i
 ≤Σ_i ρ_i^s ρ_i
 =Σ_i ρ_i^(s+1).
Indicator summands are measurable, hence AEMeasurable as required by B008. The second inequality uses inclusion and the monotonicity of a measure. All powers are nonnegative; ρ_i is finite; the power identity holds also for ρ_i=0 because s>0. These inequalities hold in ℝ≥0∞, and do not require c or the series to be finite. Taking the infimum over the arbitrary covers gives C^s_δ(A)≤C^(s+1)_δ(A×I). Taking suprema over δ and using paragraph 1 gives H^s(A)≤H^(s+1)(A×I).

5. Finite dimensions and the fibre bound (part of B104). By B003 and B004,
0≤D≤dimH(X)=finrank ℝ X=n.
The rank equality follows from the n standard Euclidean coordinate vectors; for n=0 it is the empty basis. Thus D is finite and may be identified with its nonnegative real value without changing addition or order. The same argument in X×ℝ gives dimH F≤n+1<∞ in the maximum norm; its coordinate basis has n+1 vectors.

The set I has nonempty real interior: (0,1)⊆interior I and, for example, 1/2 belongs to it. B012 with finrank ℝ ℝ=1 gives dimH I=1. Choose x₀∈E using the original nonemptiness assumption. The map t↦(x₀,t) is an isometry for the maximum product metric, since max(dist(x₀,x₀),|t-u|)=|t-u|. B006 and B003 therefore give dimH F≥dimH({x₀}×I)=1. This also proves the entire required lower bound when D=0.

6. Upper dimension inequality (part of B104). For any real q>D, we have q>0. Regard q as a nonnegative real when invoking B002. Its critical-exponent zero conclusion gives H^q(E)=0. Paragraph 3 gives H^(q+1)(F)=0, so this measure is not ∞ and B002 gives dimH F≤q+1. This holds for every q>D. Because D and dimH F are finite, it implies dimH F≤D+1: if dimH F>D+1, choose q strictly between D and dimH F-1, contradicting dimH F≤q+1. No assumption n≥1 has been made, so this includes n=0.

7. Lower dimension inequality (completion of B104). If D>0, choose any real s with 0<s<D. B002 gives H^s(E)=∞. Paragraph 4 gives H^(s+1)(F)≥H^s(E)=∞, so H^(s+1)(F)=∞. B002 now yields dimH F≥s+1. Together with the fibre bound this implies dimH F≥D+1: if instead dimH F<D+1, the fibre bound gives dimH F-1≥0, and one can choose s strictly between dimH F-1 and D, a contradiction. If D=0, paragraph 5 already gives dimH F≥D+1. Combined with paragraph 6 this proves the maximum-norm equality for every n and the original nonempty compact E. Compactness is retained as H even though the replacement cover argument needs no further use of it.

8. Return to the specified Euclidean target (B105). The header defines euclideanLift n as the identity on pairs into WithLp 2 (Rn(n)×ℝ). The prepared adapter B011 is an actual closed Lean proof from B005 using the inverse of WithLp.prodContinuousLinearEquiv 2 ℝ (Rn n) ℝ. Its underlying function is exactly euclideanLift, and it proves that every image set has the same Hausdorff dimension as in the maximum norm. This is an explicit metric-change justification, valid for all n≥0 and all sets.

B013 shows that the norm in this new space satisfies ‖(x,t)‖²=‖x‖²+|t|². Apply it to differences. In Rn(n), the squared Euclidean norm is Σ_{j<n}|x_j|² by the defining Euclidean norm. Consequently coordinate concatenation j(x,t)=(x₀,…,x_(n-1),t) has
dist(j(x,t),j(y,u))²=Σ_{j<n}|x_j-y_j|²+|t-u|²
=dist(euclideanLift(x,t),euclideanLift(y,u))².
Distances are nonnegative, so equality of squares gives equality of distances. This proves an isometry into Euclidean ℝ^(n+1); truncation of the first n coordinates and extraction of the last coordinate give its inverse. For n=0 the sum is empty and the same construction is the usual identification of ℝ^0×ℝ with ℝ. It sends euclideanLift '' (E×I) exactly to the original Euclidean product set. B006 preserves its dimension. Applying B011 and paragraph 7 therefore gives, in precisely the selected Euclidean metric,
dim_H(E×[0,1])=dim_H E+1.
The right side is the original dimension of E in the Euclidean metric of ℝ^n. All dimensions here are finite, so the ℝ≥0∞ equality is the same equality of real dimensions in the original statement. This completes the full target without residual textbook premises.

namespace BasisObjects
abbrev Rn (n : ℕ) := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)
noncomputable def content {X : Type*} [EMetricSpace X]
    (s : ℝ) (r : ℝ≥0∞) (A : Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨅ (U : ℕ → Set X) (_ : A ⊆ ⋃ i, U i)
    (_ : ∀ i, Metric.ediam (U i) ≤ r),
      ∑' i, ⨆ (_ : (U i).Nonempty), (Metric.ediam (U i)) ^ s
def euclideanLift (n : ℕ) : Rn n × ℝ → WithLp 2 (Rn n × ℝ) :=
  WithLp.toLp 2
end BasisObjects

R008.justification: In the extended nonnegative reals b≤b+1=a<∞, so b is finite. The finite part of [0,∞] is the nonnegative reals with its usual addition and unit; equality and this finite sum therefore pass to the real representatives. In S002 take a=dimH(G)=T and b=D.

1: # Lean implementation safeguards
2: 
3: Apply these requirements within the accepted NL0 and the fixed Lean interface.
4: They govern implementation, not additional NL0 detail or a weaker Audit B.
5: Use existing library readers and local checking tools; no separate review
6: model, new premise or mandatory lookup of every familiar declaration is needed.
7: 
8: 1. **Check critical library signatures.** Before relying on a critical or
9:    unfamiliar library application, establish its complete type in the pinned
10:    environment, including explicit, implicit and instance binders and all
11:    side conditions. Read the declaration or check a small typed application
12:    when its signature is uncertain. Do not infer the calling convention from
13:    its name or pass an implicit argument as though it were an explicit one.
14:    A previously checked signature in this context need not be looked up again.
15: 2. **Constrain difficult inference.** When coercions or implicit inference
16:    obscure the intended application, give the intermediate fact an explicit
17:    type and supply the relevant named parameters, such as the set, exponent
18:    or ambient space. Prefer this to leaving Lean to discover those choices by
19:    unfolding large definitions. Routine unambiguous arguments can stay
20:    implicit; explicit parameters must preserve the existing target and inputs.
21: 3. **Check conversions before combining them.** When an argument crosses Lean
22:    representations, first establish a small typed conversion fact, then use
23:    it in the main proof. In particular, distinguish `ℝ`, `ℝ≥0` and `ℝ≥0∞`;
24:    check the conversion direction, nonnegativity and any finiteness conditions.
25:    A conversion is not automatically invertible, and matching notation does
26:    not establish equality of differently typed expressions. Reuse a checked
27:    fact when available. Do not invent another representation, a global helper
28:    requirement or an extra hypothesis just to satisfy this instruction.
29: 4. **Isolate an inference failure.** If compiler feedback identifies a library
30:    application, coercion or expensive inference problem, reduce the next check
31:    to that application or conversion with explicit local types before adding
32:    more proof code. Use `check_auxiliary` in a proof worker, or
33:    `check_lean_types` during preparation when that tool is supplied. Helpers
34:    use only the current allowed inputs and never become new premises. Once
35:    the small check succeeds, integrate the result and recheck the complete
36:    obligation; success of a helper alone does not accept the target.
37: 
38: 5. **Repair after a bounded check.** Native checks have a separate per-call wall
39:    limit, normally 180 seconds, and use the controller-owned 20,000,000 heartbeat budget.
40:    A timeout or heartbeat diagnostic leaves the goal unaccepted and returns
41:    control to the same worker. Inspect the retained candidate and diagnostic,
42:    then check a smaller typed application, conversion or proof fragment before
43:    integrating it. Do not repeat the unchanged expensive candidate or disable
44:    limits to avoid diagnosis. Preserve the target, allowed inputs and proof
45:    requirements; a timeout alone establishes no mathematical gap.
46: 
47: The runtime enforces the per-call wall limit independently of these writing
48: rules. Whole-case and model-stage execution remain unlimited by default.
49: Retain failed attempts and actual diagnostics. Standalone assembly, native
50: trust/signature checks and final machine Audit B remain required.
51: 
52: Before freeze, every complete T declaration must elaborate with exactly its
53: worker parameters, instances and direct inputs. Explicitly supply parameters
54: that their argument types cannot determine; a same-named context variable is
55: not an inference rule. The strict declaration check defines the proposition,
56: without proving it, and rejects unresolved holes and non-proposition goals.
57: `#check` is a useful reader aid, not sufficient declaration acceptance. A proof
58: body cannot resolve a hole in its preceding theorem declaration.
59: 
60: Checked auxiliary propositions receive a `yui_aux_...` name and an explicit
61: application with the existing local parameters/inputs. Reuse these theorems in
62: later auxiliary checks and the final body. The controller retains their actual
63: proof bodies and compiles them into standalone assembly. They are same-node
64: implementation lemmas, not extra assumptions. Read the helper index after a
65: context reset; never rebuild a checked helper merely because a turn ended.
66: 
67: Separate diagnostic printing from proving. `show_term` and similar suggestion
68: output may spend substantial time after the proof tactic runs. If that diagnostic
69: wrapper is implicated, check the same proof without it; only the new successful
70: check establishes acceptance. Do not ignore an unsuccessful process exit. If
71: small helpers pass but a monolithic body exhausts resources, retain the separate
72: checked helper declarations and compose them rather than repeatedly copying
73: their bodies into a growing proof.

48: forgets the norm structure on `V`; it is up to downstream users to implement the L`p` norm (for
49: instance, on `Prod` and finite `Pi` types). -/
50: structure WithLp (p : ℝ≥0∞) (V : Type*) where
51:   /-- Converts an element of `V` to an element of `WithLp p V`. -/
52:   toLp (p) ::
53:   /-- Converts an element of `WithLp p V` to an element of `V`. -/

62: meta def WithLp.delabToLp : Delab := delabApp

71: @[simps]
72: protected def equiv : WithLp p V ≃ V where
73:   toFun := ofLp
74:   invFun := toLp p
75:   left_inv _ := rfl
76:   right_inv _ := rfl

483: for `0` and `⊤` (i.e., `0 ^ x = 0` for `x > 0`, `1` for `x = 0` and `⊤` for `x < 0`, and

1: # Hausdorff dimension of a product with an interval
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: Elias M. Stein and Rami Shakarchi, *Real Analysis: Measure Theory,
6: Integration, and Hilbert Spaces*, Princeton Lectures in Analysis III,
7: Chapter 7, Problems, exercise 9, printed page 388.
8: Book DOI: [10.1515/9781400835560](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400835560).
9: 
10: > 9. Let \(E\) be a compact set in \(\mathbb R^{d-1}\). Show that
11: > \(\dim(E\times I)=\dim(E)+1\), where \(I\) is the unit interval in
12: > \(\mathbb R\).
13: 
14: ## Fixed interpretation and complete target
15: 
16: Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
17: 2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
18: \(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
19: the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.
20: 
21: Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
22: compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
23: with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove
24: 
25: \[
26: \dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
27: \]
28: 
29: The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
30: formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
31: 
32: ## Fixed natural-language proof
33: 
34: For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put
35: 
36: \[
37: H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
38:  A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
39: \qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
40: \]
41: 
42: Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero. This
43: unnormalized Hausdorff measure gives the usual Hausdorff dimension. We use
44: its critical-exponent characterization: \(H^s(A)=0\) if
45: \(s>\dim_H A\), and \(H^s(A)=\infty\) if \(0<s<\dim_H A\).
46: Conversely, zero measure implies \(\dim_H A\leq s\), and infinite
47: measure implies \(\dim_H A\geq s\).
48: 
49: Write \(D=\dim_H E\) and \(F=E\times[0,1]\). First \(0\leq D\leq n\).
50: Indeed, compactness makes \(E\) bounded. When \(n>0\), a box containing
51: it admits a cover by at most \(Ch^{-n}\) cubes of side at most \(h\),
52: for \(0<h\leq1\). Here \(C\) depends only on that box. Each cube has
53: diameter at most \(\sqrt n h\). For any \(s>n\), the total \(s\)-cost
54: is at most \(C n^{s/2}h^{s-n}\to0\). These arbitrarily fine covers
55: give \(H^s(E)=0\) and hence \(D\leq n\). If \(n=0\), nonemptiness
56: makes \(E=\mathbb R^0\), a singleton of zero \(s\)-cost for every
57: \(s>0\); thus \(D=0\).
58: 
59: ### Upper bound
60: 
61: When \(n=0\), \(F\) is isometric to \([0,1]\). Dividing this interval
62: into \(N\) equal pieces gives total \(a\)-cost \(N^{1-a}\to0\) for
63: every \(a>1\), proving \(\dim_H F\leq1=D+1\).
64: For this upper-bound argument now assume \(n\geq1\).
65: 
66: Fix \(q>D\). Since \(q>0\) and \(H^q(E)=0\), for every
67: \(0<r\leq1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a countable cover
68: \((U_i)\) of \(E\) with nonempty-member diameters
69: \(0<r_i\leq r\) and \(\sum_i r_i^q<\varepsilon\).
70: The positive-diameter requirement costs nothing: start with a cover of
71: cost below \(\varepsilon/2\); replace each zero-diameter singleton by
72: a ball of diameter at most \(r\), choosing the \(i\)-th replacement
73: to have \(q\)-cost less than \(\varepsilon2^{-i-2}\). The added cost
74: is less than \(\varepsilon/2\). Discard empty members.
75: 
76: Let \(N_i=\lceil1/r_i\rceil\). Partition \([0,1]\) into \(N_i\)
77: closed intervals of length \(1/N_i\leq r_i\). Because \(r_i\leq1\),
78: \(N_i\leq2/r_i\). The corresponding products with \(U_i\) form a
79: countable cover of \(F\). Each has Euclidean diameter at most
80: \(\sqrt2 r_i\), and their total \((q+1)\)-cost is at most
81: 
82: \[
83: \sum_iN_i(\sqrt2 r_i)^{q+1}
84: \leq2(\sqrt2)^{q+1}\sum_i r_i^q
85: <2(\sqrt2)^{q+1}\varepsilon.
86: \]
87: 
88: For any target scale \(\delta>0\), choose
89: \(r\leq\min(1,\delta/\sqrt2)\), then let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
90: Thus \(H^{q+1}_\delta(F)=0\) for every scale, so

91: \(H^{q+1}(F)=0\) and \(\dim_H F\leq q+1\). Letting \(q\downarrow D\)
92: gives \(\dim_H F\leq D+1\).
93: 
94: ### Lower bound when \(D>0\)
95: 
96: Fix \(0<s<D\). Then \(H^s(E)=\infty\), so
97: \(H^s_\delta(E)\) becomes arbitrarily large as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
98: We claim that, for every \(\delta>0\),
99: 
100: \[
101: H^s_\delta(E)\leq H^{s+1}_\delta(F).                 \tag{1}
102: \]
103: 
104: Take an arbitrary countable \(\delta\)-cover \((V_i)_{i\geq0}\) of
105: \(F\), discarding empty members. Define
106: \(\rho_i=\operatorname{diam}V_i\),
107: \(A_i=\pi_{\mathbb R^n}(V_i)\), and
108: \(B_i=\pi_{\mathbb R}(V_i)\). Coordinate projections are 1-Lipschitz,
109: so both projected diameters are at most \(\rho_i\leq\delta\).
110: For \(\varepsilon>0\), put
111: 
112: \[
113: \eta_i=\frac{\varepsilon2^{-i-1}}{1+\rho_i^s}>0.
114: \]
115: 
116: Enclose \(B_i\) in an open interval \(J_i\) of length at most
117: \(\rho_i+\eta_i\): its supremum minus infimum is at most \(\rho_i\),
118: and an enlargement of total width \(\eta_i\) suffices. This avoids
119: assuming that the arbitrary covering sets or their projections are measurable.
120: 
121: For each \(t\in[0,1]\), the sets \(A_i\) for which \(t\in J_i\)
122: cover \(E\). Indeed, a point \((x,t)\in F\) belongs to some \(V_i\),
123: giving \(x\in A_i\) and \(t\in B_i\subset J_i\). Their diameters
124: are at most \(\rho_i\). Consequently, with \(c=H^s_\delta(E)\),
125: 
126: \[
127: c\leq\sum_i\rho_i^s\mathbf1_{J_i}(t)\quad(t\in[0,1]).
128: \]
129: 
130: The constant \(c\) is finite: compactness gives a finite cover of \(E\)
131: by balls of diameter at most \(\delta\), with finite \(s\)-cost.
132: Each summand is nonnegative and measurable since \(J_i\) is open.
133: Integrate over \([0,1]\), of Lebesgue measure one, and use Tonelli's
134: theorem for this nonnegative series. Since
135: \(|J_i\cap[0,1]|\leq\rho_i+\eta_i\),
136: 
137: \[
138: \begin{aligned}
139: c&\leq\sum_i\rho_i^s|J_i\cap[0,1]|\\
140:  &\leq\sum_i\rho_i^{s+1}+\sum_i\eta_i\rho_i^s
141:  \leq\sum_i\rho_i^{s+1}+\varepsilon.
142: \end{aligned}
143: \]
144: 
145: If the first series is infinite the desired inequality is immediate;
146: otherwise let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Take the infimum over the
147: arbitrary covers to obtain (1). As its left side is unbounded at small
148: scales, \(H^{s+1}(F)=\infty\), giving \(\dim_H F\geq s+1\).
149: Letting \(s\uparrow D\) proves \(\dim_H F\geq D+1\).
150: 
151: ### Lower bound when \(D=0\)
152: 
153: Choose \(x_0\in E\). The map \(t\mapsto(x_0,t)\) is an isometric
